## Symptom

First production run, 2026-08-07:

```
agento11y: push rejected as unauthorized (this will not fix itself): 401:
{"status":"error","error":"authentication error: invalid scope requested"}
```

The endpoint and region are right - `agento11y-prod-gb-south-1.grafana.net` resolves to a sigil ELB, and the same host/credentials work for OTLP traces. It is the scope.

## Cause

`ExportGenerations` needs **`sigil:write`** on the access policy. The token in `/opt/codexlb2otel/.env` is the shared one copied from the sibling exporters and carries logs/metrics/traces write only.

Source for the scope name: gcx's own `agento11y-instrument` skill, which also carries the trap - **in the Cloud UI, `sigil` is not in the default resource list.** It has to be added via **"Add scope"**, then tick Write. The Cloud resource kept the old name even though the product is now Agent Observability, so searching for "agento11y" finds nothing.

## Why this blocked everything, not just sigil

The sink classifies a 401 as a **config fault**: never retried, and the error propagates, so the watcher holds the checkpoint. That is the right call for a credential that will never fix itself - but it means one missing scope stops Loki, metrics and traces too. Combined with #29 the service ingested nothing at all.

Now ships `agento11y.enabled: false` (`ec6ecbc`), so the other three signals run. The example config carries the full turn-on instructions inline, and `TestLoad_ExampleConfigIsDeployable` asserts it stays false, so flipping it is a decision made with the credential in hand rather than an accident.

## To close

- [ ] Add `sigil:write` to the access policy (or mint a token from the stack's `grafana-agento11y-app` plugin → Connection tab, with sigil/metrics/traces/logs write), and update `/opt/codexlb2otel/.env`.
- [ ] Flip `agento11y.enabled` to true in `config.example.yaml`, redeploy it to `/opt/codex-lb/codexlb2otel.config.yaml`, and update the assertion in `TestLoad_ExampleConfigIsDeployable`.
- [ ] Confirm generations actually arrive: `gcx --context m7kni agento11y generations list`. A 2xx is not enough here - `ExportGenerations` can accept the request and still refuse individual generations, which is why `accountResults` parses the per-generation verdicts.

**Rob's action, not something this repo can do** - minting or rescoping an access policy needs Cloud admin credentials that are not wired into any tooling here.
title: agento11y needs the sigil:write scope; the token has only logs/metrics/traces

body:
Fixed by `ec6ecbc`. Filed after the fact so the diagnosis is not only in a commit message.

## Symptom

First production run on camden, 2026-08-07. Every poll, forever:

```
level=ERROR msg="poll failed" err="read 2026-08-06T18.jsonl.gz: flush: otlpmetric: otlpmetric: flush: context deadline exceeded"
```

Nothing reached Mimir. The checkpoint never advanced - correctly, since a failed flush must hold it - so the same chunk was re-read every 30s and no archive file was ever reclaimed. It read as a network timeout against the OTLP gateway. It was not one.

## Cause

`Poll` holds `mu` for the whole pass. Inside that pass:

1. `emit` → `sinkEmit` → `otlpmetric.Sink.Flush`
2. → `MeterProvider.ForceFlush` → reader `Collect`
3. → the SDK runs the registered **async-instrument callback**
4. → that callback is `internal/selfobs` asking **this same watcher** for `Progress()`
5. → `Progress()` took `mu.RLock()`

A read lock cannot be acquired while the calling goroutine's own stack already holds the write lock. `Collect` blocked until the `PeriodicReader`'s **default 30s timeout** fired, and the flush failed. Self-observability - the feature whose entire job is to surface failures first - was the failure.

Two things made it look like something else. The 30s is the **reader's** default, not `otlp.timeout`, so raising `otlp.timeout` changed nothing and the number looked like a coincidence. And a blocked `Collect` surfaces as `context deadline exceeded`, which is exactly what a slow network produces.

## How it was narrowed

By elimination, since the error named the wrong subsystem:

| test | result | rules out |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1MiB read chunk instead of 16MiB | fails identically at 30.0s | payload size |
| `otlp.timeout: 90s` | still fails at **30.0s** | the exporter's own timeout |
| exporter retries disabled | still fails at 30.0s | retry-until-deadline on 429/5xx |
| empty OTLP metrics POST, same URL + credentials | **200 in 0.5s** | auth, endpoint, reachability |
| count data points from one archive via `ManualReader` | **132 points, Collect < 1ms** | cardinality, collection cost |
| same binary with `RegisterSelfObs` disabled | **19 chunks, every flush succeeded** | everything else |

The last row is the proof; the rest is why it took that long to get there.

## Fix

`Progress()` now takes **no lock**. The watcher publishes a snapshot under the write lock at the end of each pass (and at construction, so a collection arriving before the first poll reads a zero value rather than a half-initialised one) and `Progress()` reads it through an `atomic.Pointer`. A reader sees state as of the last completed pass instead of a half-finished one, which for an operational metric is not a cost.

Regression test: `TestWatcher_ProgressIsSafeFromInsideEmit` calls `Progress` from inside the emit callback and bounds `Poll` at 10s - the failure mode is "never returns", so an unbounded call would wedge the suite instead of failing it. Mutation-checked by restoring the `RLock`, which fails it at the 10s bound.

## Why no test caught it

Both halves were tested, neither together. `internal/tail`'s tests drive `Poll` with an emit callback that does nothing. `internal/sink/otlpmetric`'s selfobs tests use a `ManualReader` and call `Collect` from the test goroutine, holding no watcher lock. The deadlock only exists where the two meet, which until this commit was only in `main`.

The general shape worth remembering: **a callback registered with a library is code the library calls on a goroutine and at a moment of its choosing - including re-entrantly, from inside a call you made.** Any lock held across that call is a lock the callback must not take.

## Not caused by this, but found with it

`agento11y` 401s with `authentication error: invalid scope requested` - see #30. The sink correctly treats that as a config fault and holds the checkpoint, which means one missing scope stops every other signal too. Now ships disabled.

comments.body:
## Verified in production

`ec6ecbc` deployed to camden, then `cdcf80d` on top. Zero errors since.

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| poll outcome | `context deadline exceeded` at 30.0s, every poll | clean, every poll |
| bytes ingested | 0 | **2,209 MB** (the whole 22-file backlog, first pass, ~5 min) |
| `codexlb_selfobs_ingest_lag_seconds` | absent | **4.7s** — poll interval is 5s, so it is caught up |
| files reclaimed | 0 | 6, all `reason=retain_days` |

Signals confirmed by reading them back rather than by the absence of errors:

- **Mimir** — `codexlb_turns_total` 5,530, `codexlb_tokens_total` 1.4e9, all 16 `codexlb_selfobs_*` series present.
- **Tempo** — root service `codexlb2otel`, root span `turn`, 142 spans in the sampled trace.
- **Loki** — steadily rising, 60→185 lines/min over the sampled window.
- **Retention** — every 2026-08-06 file fully read and deleted, every 2026-08-07 file kept. Checkpoint shows offset == size on all 22.

### One thing the fix initially got wrong, fixed by `cdcf80d`

A pass reads every file to EOF, so the first one after a restart works the entire backlog in a single call. Publishing the snapshot only at the *end* of a pass meant every progress metric read zero for that whole window, and the two gated on having seen any data - ingest lag and current-file offset - were **absent from Mimir outright**. That is exactly the window someone is watching. Now republished per accepted chunk.

Worth noting because it is the same shape as the bug itself: the first fix was correct and still left self-observability blind at the one moment it mattered.

### Loki drops on the backlog are expected, not a regression

`codexlb_selfobs_sink_rejections_total{sink="loki", reason="too_old"}` = **29,771**. The backlog is older than `loki.max_line_age` (3h), so the sink drops those lines locally rather than letting Loki discard them server-side behind a 204. Recent data flows normally. This is the designed behaviour and the counter is doing its job - but it does mean **the log half of the backlog is gone for good**, which is worth knowing before anyone reads a historical dashboard and concludes ingestion was broken.

body:
## Intent

Rob, 2026-08-07: move codex-lb's conversation archive off local disk onto a memory-backed filesystem, then consume it and prune anything older than X hours (or drop the whole prior day). This issue records the sizing, the traps, and the decision this forces about `:ro`.

## Sizing - it fits comfortably

Measured on camden 2026-08-07:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| archive on disk | 2.1 GiB, 20 files, oldest `2026-08-06T18`, newest `2026-08-07T19` |
| rate | ~80 MiB/hour average, ~2 GiB/day |
| per-file spread | 5 MiB to 84 MiB in the sampled window - highly variable with usage |
| camden RAM | 124 GiB total, 101 GiB available, 81 GiB already in buff/cache |
| existing tmpfs | `/tmp` and `/dev/shm` at 63 GiB each, both near-empty |

24h of retention costs ~2 GiB of RAM. Even a week is ~14 GiB. This is not the constraint.

**Cap the tmpfs explicitly.** A tmpfs with no `size=` defaults to 50% of RAM (62 GiB here). Size it for the retention window plus a wide margin - see the ENOSPC trap below for why the cap has to be deliberate rather than inherited.

Note camden's swap is zram (8 GiB, 4.3 GiB in use). tmpfs pages under pressure go to compressed RAM, and gzip data does not compress again, so zram buys nothing here - budget the tmpfs as if it were pinned RAM.

## The decision this actually forces

Today the archive on disk is the **durable record** and everything shipped to Grafana Cloud is a derived view. On tmpfs with pruning, that inverts: Grafana Cloud becomes the only copy of anything outside the window, and a reboot drops whatever has not been ingested.

That may be exactly right - the archive stops being an archive and becomes a **buffer** - but it should be a deliberate call, because:

- **A 2xx is not delivery** in any of the three protocols this service speaks (Loki 204s a discarded line, sigil reports `partial_success`, ExportGenerations returns per-generation verdicts). An ingest outage longer than the window is silent permanent loss.
- Ingest has never run against a real archive yet. `codexlb.selfobs.ingest_lag_seconds` exists precisely to catch this and has zero production observations.

**If the answer is "yes, it's a buffer", then the `:ro` mount constraint dissolves with it.** #10's hard rule - this service must never be able to damage the archive - was justified by the archive being the only copy of the raw capture. Once it is not, the rule is protecting a temp file.

## Who owns the deletion

The two candidates differ on one thing that matters: whether deletion knows how far ingest has got.

**Age-based external pruning is blind.** `systemd-tmpfiles`, a cron `find -mmin +X -delete`, a boot-time wipe - all key on mtime alone. If codexlb2otel is down, crashlooping, or behind, they delete data that was never shipped. On tmpfs there is no second copy to go back to.

**`reclaim()` is not blind.** `internal/tail/watcher.go:443` requires three conditions, all of them: the file is fully consumed (`offset >= size`, `size > 0`), it is not the chronologically newest file (the one codex-lb is still appending to - `offset == size` there only means we have caught up), and its mtime is older than `delete_after`. It is implemented, tested (`watcher_test.go:215`, and `:242` pins that a zero `delete_after` deletes nothing), and marks `Deleted` in the checkpoint so a reappearing file is not re-read.

So:

- **Option A - codexlb2otel owns it.** Drop `:ro`, set `archive.delete_after`. Safe by construction, zero new moving parts, already built. Costs the write-access constraint, which the tmpfs decision above has already spent.
- **Option B - external pruner, `:ro` kept.** Must gate on ingest progress rather than age: read `/var/lib/codexlb2otel/checkpoint.json` (it carries per-file `offset`/`size`/`deleted`) or gate on the health endpoint. New component, new failure mode, duplicates logic that already exists.

**Recommendation: A.** B is only worth it if the `:ro` constraint survives the move to tmpfs, and the reasoning above says it does not.

Note that as things stand today the config knob is doubly disabled: `delete_after: 0s` is the default and what is deployed, **and** the mount is `:ro`, so `os.Remove` returns `EROFS`. Verified on a throwaway directory on camden 2026-08-07: `rm: can't remove '/a/a': Read-only file system`. Setting `delete_after` alone would produce one error log per poll and reclaim nothing.

## "Older than X hours" beats "delete the prior day"

Files are hourly (`2026-08-07T19.jsonl.gz`), so both are expressible. Age-based gives a uniform floor on how far behind ingest can fall before data is lost. Whole-prior-day makes that floor swing between 0 and 24 hours depending on when the failure starts, and the worst case lands just before midnight. Age-based also maps straight onto `reclaim`'s existing mtime check with no new code.

## Traps to design against

- **tmpfs full is codex-lb's problem, not a disk-usage problem.** If pruning is gated on ingest and ingest stalls, files accumulate to the cap and then codex-lb's own archive writes start failing with ENOSPC. The observability plumbing must not be able to take down the thing it observes. Size generously and alert on tmpfs utilisation, not just on ingest lag.
- **The mount must carry ownership.** codex-lb writes the archive as uid 1000 with mode 0700, and codexlb2otel now runs as `user: "1000:1000"` for exactly that reason (#10). A tmpfs is recreated empty on every boot, so `uid=1000,gid=1000,mode=0700` has to be in the mount options - a one-time `chown` does not survive a reboot.
- **The checkpoint's file map is never pruned.** `cp.Files` gains an entry per archive filename ever seen and nothing removes them (`internal/tail/checkpoint.go`). It is rewritten on every poll, so with hourly files it grows ~8,760 entries/year. Small today, unbounded, and the tmpfs plan makes disappearing files the normal case rather than the exception. Worth capping or aging out as part of this work.
- **Filename reuse is real and already handled - do not regress it.** codex-lb reopens the archive `O_APPEND|O_CREAT` per batch, so the same name can be two different files (`2026-08-06T18` was observed as two, covering 18:00-18:27 and 18:43-18:52). Content fingerprinting catches it; size comparison alone does not.
- **`/mnt/codex-lb-archive` already exists and is empty.** The NFS mount to the Synology is up but unused, and codex-lb's compose carries a stale comment claiming the archive lives there via `CODEX_LB_CONVERSATION_ARCHIVE_DIR` - a variable that is not set. If the answer to "do we keep a durable copy" is yes, that mount is the obvious destination and the comment stops being a lie.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decide explicitly: is the archive a durable record or a buffer? Record the answer and the reason here.
- [ ] If buffer: revisit #10's `:ro` constraint in the same breath, with the reasoning written down.
- [ ] tmpfs mounted with an explicit `size=`, `uid=1000,gid=1000,mode=0700`, in `/etc/fstab` so it survives a reboot.
- [ ] Retention expressed as an age, wired to whichever owner is chosen.
- [ ] Deletion gated on ingest progress, not on mtime alone.
- [ ] Alert on tmpfs utilisation as well as on `codexlb2otel.selfobs.ingest_lag_seconds`.
- [ ] Checkpoint file-map growth bounded.
- [ ] Do not attempt any of this before ingest has run against a real archive for long enough to trust it. Pruning an unproven pipeline is how the raw capture gets lost.

comments.body:
## Decided and implemented - `f937dee`, closed

Rob overrode the framing in the body: *"it's not that deep for this internal tool so yeah we want anything from the prior day and older to get deleted simple date comparison and delete and make it so it works within the container it's okay for yesterdays and older to be gone this is a me only tool"*.

So of the two questions this issue posed, both are answered: the archive is a **buffer**, not a durable record, and codexlb2otel **owns the deletion** (Option A). The elaborate acceptance list in the body is deliberately not what got built - it was scoped for a durability requirement that does not exist.

### What landed

`archive.retain_days` - keep N UTC calendar days counting today, `1` = today alone. Set to `1` in `config.example.yaml` and deployed to camden. `delete_after` stays as the rolling-duration alternative; either rule firing reclaims a file, and both being available is not a contradiction.

Not folded into `delete_after`, because a calendar boundary and a rolling duration give different answers: at 09:00, "anything over 24h old" still keeps half of yesterday. That is not what "delete yesterday" means.

**UTC, and this is the part that would have been wrong by default.** codex-lb builds the name as `datetime.now(UTC).strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H')` - read out of `/opt/codex-lb/src/app/core/conversation_archive.py:170`, not inferred, and corroborated by mtimes (the file named `2026-08-07T17` was last written at `18:59:59 +0100`). Local-time arithmetic is invisible in Britain for half the year and deletes the current day's early files anywhere west of Greenwich. Pinned by `TestWatcher_RetainDaysIsUTC`, which swaps `time.Local` to New York at 00:30 UTC and asserts the prior UTC day still goes. Mutation-checked: flipping the implementation to `.Local()` fails it.

**Two guards, not configurable.** A file is never deleted until fully read, so a restart behind a backlog ingests the backlog before dropping any of it - the one case where deletion and ingest genuinely disagree, and the only place worth spending code. And the newest file is never touched, since codex-lb is still appending to it.

### `:ro` reversed

The archive mount is now read-write, on both the repo fragment and `/opt/codex-lb/compose.yml`. #10's read-only rule was justified by the archive being the only copy of the raw capture; it is a buffer now, so the justification went with it. `docker compose config` confirms `read_only: true` is gone from the resolved mount.

Left read-only, `os.Remove` returns EROFS and the result is one error log per poll and zero reclaimed bytes - so `codexlb.selfobs.files_reclaimed`'s description now says a flat counter means deletion is **failing**, not that nothing was due.

### Also

Added a test that `config.example.yaml` loads and validates. It is copied verbatim onto camden as the deployed config and nothing checked it, while a misspelled yaml key fails silently: the field keeps its `Default()` value and the setting is ignored - which for `retain_days` means the disk quietly never gets reclaimed. Deployed file verified identical to the repo's by md5.

### Not done, on purpose

The **tmpfs move itself** is a host change and is not needed for any of the above - retention works the same on local disk, which is where the archive is today. Whenever the mount moves, `uid=1000,gid=1000,mode=0700` and an explicit `size=` still apply (a tmpfs comes back empty every boot, so a one-time `chown` does not survive), and the ENOSPC-hits-codex-lb risk from the body is still real. Reopen or file fresh at that point.

Checkpoint file-map growth is still unbounded and is now more relevant, not less, since deleted files become the normal case. Small (~8,760 entries/year, marked `deleted`), so not worth blocking on - noted here rather than left as a surprise.

## What happens

`publish.yml` delegates to the fleet's shared `rknightion/.github` `container-publish.yml`. Everything works except the final step:

```
Error: Failed to persist attestation: Feature not available for user-owned
private repositories. To enable this feature, please make this repository public.
```

**The image still publishes.** The per-arch builds, the manifest-list merge, the GHCR push and the cosign signature all succeed; only `actions/attest-build-provenance` fails, after the image is already usable. Verified on the current `:main`:

```
mediaType: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json
  linux/arm64  sha256:c0e5d583e17ca053fc9
  linux/amd64  sha256:c2588319b179ea91a9a
```

So camden and watchtower are unaffected — this is a red run, not a broken pipeline.

## Why it cannot be fixed from this repo

The attestation step in the shared workflow is **unconditional**. Its inputs gate `sbom`, `sign`, `trivy`, `dockerhub-login` and `otel-tracing`, but there is no `attest` input, so a caller cannot switch it off. Every sibling `*2otel` repo is public, which is why none of them hits this.

## Decision, 2026-08-07: leave it red for now

Rob's call, recorded so it is not re-litigated. The two real fixes were considered and deliberately not taken:

- **Make this repo public.** Would resolve it outright and match the rest of the fleet. History was checked and is clean — no `.jsonl`/`.gz` has ever been committed on any ref, no `.env` or key either, `internal/fixture/tracked_test.go` guards it going forward, and `corpus.sig.json` is content-free by construction (audited during #21, when descending into embedded JSON briefly exposed a home-directory layout and private repo names before that was closed). Not taken now because making a repo public is effectively irreversible: the history can be cloned and cached even if the setting is flipped back.
- **Add an `attest` input upstream** to `rknightion/.github`'s `container-publish.yml`, defaulting true, and pin to a new version here. Not taken because it is a fleet-wide change to another repo for one caller's benefit.

## The cost of leaving it

A permanently-red publish run trains everyone to ignore publish failures, which is exactly how the next real one gets missed. Two real bugs were already caught in this workflow today by it going red — a missing `contents: read` and a missing version tag — and neither would have been noticed if red were the normal state.

So this should not stay open indefinitely. Revisit when either the repo goes public or the shared workflow gains the input.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Publish runs are green, by whichever route
- [ ] Multi-arch `:main` and the semver release tags keep working
- [ ] cosign signing and SBOM generation keep working

Refs #10

Found while building #14's dashboards, and it blocks one of that issue's acceptance criteria.

## The problem

codex-lb's health probes **deliberately exercise the real models**. #14 says so explicitly and adds: they "cannot be separated by model - only by `family`". So `codexlb.family` is the only way to keep synthetic traffic out of a cost or latency panel.

`internal/sink/otlpmetric/record.go` attaches `attr.Family` to exactly two instruments: `codexlb.transport_events` and `codexlb.baseline_resets`. Every other instrument narrows the base attribute set with `attr.Only(...)` and drops it:

- all token counters and the token-usage histogram
- every duration histogram - operation, turn, TTFT, engine wall, harness unblocked, sampling/stream, pre-inference, client tool pause
- the new #23 timing family - engine_service/iapi inference and sampling, the responses_excl_* variants, all three TBT histograms
- engine calls, tool calls, tool-calls-per-operation, web search, image-gen tokens

`codexlb.responses` and `codexlb.turns` do carry it, because they emit the unnarrowed base set.

## Why it matters

**Every cost and latency number this service publishes to Prometheus silently includes probe traffic**, and there is no query that can remove it. A dashboard showing p95 turn latency or tokens-per-model is mixing real user work with synthetic health checks and cannot say by how much. That is a correctness problem in the numbers, not a missing filter.

#14 worked around it for the token/cost panels by going to LogQL against the turn record's JSON body instead of PromQL, since `family` *is* structured metadata on every Loki line. That works, but it means the Prometheus panels are the ones that cannot be trusted, which is backwards - the metrics pipeline is the one built for aggregation.

## The decision this needs

Adding `codexlb.family` to those instruments multiplies their series count by the number of observed family values. Measured on the current corpus that is **3** (`websocket`, `http`, `unknown`), with `probe` seen in earlier captures, and the field is capped at 8 in the registry. So the real multiplier is 3-4 on the affected instruments.

That is a genuine cardinality cost and it is a contract decision under #3, which is why this is an issue rather than a patch.

Two other narrowed attributes are worth reviewing at the same time, since the same `attr.Only` calls are the cause:
- no token metric carries `gen_ai.request.reasoning.level` or `codexlb.thread_source`, so "token shape by effort and by user-vs-subagent" - a named #14 panel - is not answerable in PromQL either
- both are bounded and small (4 and 3 observed)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decide, with the cardinality arithmetic written down, which instruments gain `codexlb.family`
- [ ] At minimum every duration histogram and every token counter, or the probe-exclusion criterion on #14 cannot be met
- [ ] Decide the same for `reasoning.level` and `thread_source` on the token counters
- [ ] `TestEveryEmittedAttributeKeyIsOnContract` still passes; no new attribute key is invented - all three already exist in the registry
- [ ] Corpus-backed cardinality check, measured not assumed, the way #3's cap test does it
- [ ] #14's PromQL panels updated to exclude probe family by default, and its LogQL workarounds reverted where PromQL now suffices

Refs #14, #3, #23, #7
title: Probe traffic cannot be excluded from token or latency metrics - codexlb.family is stripped from all of them

#12 landed the capture (4968921) and stopped there, deliberately - its acceptance criteria were about the reducer. The fields do reach Loki for free, because `turnLine` marshals every scalar on `Turn`. They reach **no metric and no span**, which for a load balancer is where latency data actually gets used.

## What is captured but unemitted

Nine cumulative fields, delta-treated against the series baseline:

`EngineServiceInferenceMsDelta`, `EngineServiceSamplingMsDelta`, `EngineIapiInferenceMsDelta`, `EngineIapiSamplingMsDelta`, `ResponsesExclEngineAndToolMsDelta`, `ResponsesExclEngineWaitSamplingMsDelta`, `ResponsesExclEngineWaitSamplingIapiMsDelta`, `ResponsesAPIExclClientToolsMsDelta`, `EngineUncachedPromptTokensDelta`

Three per-response, never diffed (running averages, not sums):

`EngineServiceTBTMs`, `EngineIapiTBTMs`, `EngineServiceMinusIapiTBTMs`

Plus `ToolCallDurationsMs` (suffix-diffed per-tool-call array), `Temperature`, `TopP`, `Tools`, `ToolsHash`.

## What each one wants

- **The eight millisecond deltas are durations** and belong in histograms, in seconds, under the units the existing duration instruments already use. `engine_service_*` versus `engine_iapi_*` is the same measurement from two vantage points, so the pair is the interesting comparison - two instruments, or one with a domain attribute, and that is the decision this issue has to make.
- **`EngineUncachedPromptTokensDelta`** is a token counter and should join the existing `gen_ai.token.type` axis - but see the warning on `tokenTypes` in `internal/sink/otlpmetric/record.go` first: cached is a breakdown NESTED inside input, not an additive sibling, and the same trap applies here. Adding a value that naive summing double-counts is worse than not adding it.
- **The three TBT fields** are per-response averages. A histogram of an average is defensible but needs saying out loud, and `EngineServiceMinusIapiTBTMs` goes negative (min -6.70 measured), so any instrument must accept negative values or explicitly clamp and say so.
- **`ToolCallDurationsMs`** maps directly onto the existing per-tool-call spans in `internal/sink/otlptrace` - it is one duration per tool call and the spans already exist. This is the highest-value item here and probably the easiest.
- **`Temperature` / `TopP`** are span and `Generation` fields only, under the GenAI convention names. **Never metric attributes**: measured constant across the corpus at 1.0 and 0.98, so they would add a dimension with one value.
- **`Tools` / `ToolsHash`** feed sigil's `Generation.tools`. Note the limitation recorded on #22: the wire only carries a dynamically-added catalogue on 5.2% of creates and never the built-in toolset, so `effective_version` still cannot be computed.

## Cardinality

Every new instrument goes through the one shared `attr.Guard` and takes attributes from `internal/attr` only. No new attribute keys should be needed - the existing base set (`gen_ai.request.model`, `codexlb.account_id`, `codexlb.request_kind`) is the right grouping for all of these.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The eight duration deltas emitted as histograms in seconds, with the service-versus-iapi comparison expressible in one query
- [ ] `EngineUncachedPromptTokensDelta` emitted without creating a double-count under a naive sum across `gen_ai.token.type`
- [ ] The three TBT fields emitted, with the negative-value case handled explicitly rather than by accident
- [ ] `ToolCallDurationsMs` attached to the existing per-tool-call spans
- [ ] `Temperature`/`TopP` on spans and Generations, and provably not on any metric
- [ ] `TestEveryEmittedAttributeKeyIsOnContract` still passes, and no new attribute key is introduced
- [ ] Cardinality checked against the corpus, not assumed

Refs #12, #22, #7, #11

Everything here was deliberately descoped from #18 (954bd03) and #19 (d4cfe31) rather than dropped. Each is small and independent.

## 1. Reduce the tool catalogue into `Turn`

`response.create` carries `tools[]` with `.name`, `.description`, `.parameters`, `.output_schema` and `.strict` — **measured present across the full corpus**, not assumed. `internal/turn`'s `createEvent` decodes only `parallel_tool_calls` and drops the rest.

Until this lands, sigil's `Generation.tools` is always empty and any "tools available to this agent" surface in agento11y stays blank. It also blocks the backend from computing `effective_version`, which it derives from `sha256(system_prompt + sorted tools)`.

The catalogue is re-sent on every turn, so it needs the same dedup-by-hash treatment `Turn.InstructionsHash` already gets — emitting a full tool catalogue per response would be the same waste the instructions dedup exists to avoid.

- [ ] Decode `response.tools[]` onto `Turn`, deduplicated by hash
- [ ] Map to `ToolDefinition` in `internal/sink/agento11y`
- [ ] Confirm the Loki line budget still holds with a catalogue attached

## 2. `temperature` and `top_p` are on the wire and unreduced

#18 recorded these as absent; they are not. `response.temperature` and `response.top_p` are on `response.completed` and genuinely vary (they carry no `values` list in `corpus.sig.json`, which `internal/profile/signature.go` only omits above 32 distinct values). `response.max_output_tokens` is genuinely null.

`turn.Turn` has no field for either, which is why #18 could not emit them — it was a scope boundary, not a data judgment.

- [ ] Add both to `Turn`
- [ ] Emit as span attributes under the spec's names, and as `Generation.temperature`/`top_p`, which the sigil proto has as optional fields

## 3. Split an oversized batch instead of dropping it

`internal/sink/agento11y` treats a 413 as a data fault: counted, dropped, checkpoint advances. That is deliberate and correct as a floor — the alternative, holding the checkpoint, wedges the pipeline forever on a batch that can never drain.

But dropping is still data loss, and it is avoidable: halve the batch and retry, down to a single generation. Only a single generation that is itself too large is genuinely undeliverable.

- [ ] Halve-and-retry on 413 before counting a rejection
- [ ] Count only what remains undeliverable at batch size 1

## 4. `AgentMessages` have nowhere to go in a Generation

`Turn.AgentMessages` carries author/recipient task paths (`/root/lab_baseline` -> `/root`) and is the only record of the multi-agent topology anywhere in the capture. Sigil's `MessageRole` has no agent concept, but `Message.name` exists and would carry the task path.

Worth deciding rather than leaving unmapped by default.

- [ ] Decide whether an agent message is an `input`/`output` message with `name` set, or genuinely has no home in the Generation model

## 5. `ToolCall.Input` has no size bound

`ToolOutput` is truncated upstream and records `Truncated`; `ToolCall.Input` is not truncated at all. It now flows into `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments` as a span attribute, so a very large tool-call argument produces an oversized span attribute.

- [ ] Measure the actual distribution of `ToolCall.Input` sizes in the corpus before deciding whether a bound is needed

Refs #18, #19, #3

comments.body:
Items **3** and **5** landed in a13a574. Items 1, 2 and 4 remain open.

**Item 3 — halve-and-retry on 413.** `push` now splits a 413'd batch in two and retries each half, recursing to batches of one. The floor is unchanged and deliberately so: a lone generation that still 413s is counted `line_too_long` and dropped so the checkpoint advances, because holding it wedges the pipeline on a batch that can never drain. Termination is bounded rather than merely expected — `floor(n/2) < n` for all `n > 1` and the `len(gens) > 1` guard stops the recursion, so depth is at most `ceil(log2(BatchSize))`, about 8 for a 200-generation batch. Nothing is counted at intermediate split levels, so a generation is counted at most once however many times its batch was halved. A config fault reached while retrying a half propagates out unchanged; swallowing it because we are "inside a split" would let the checkpoint advance past data that never landed. Three tests: multi-level convergence with zero rejections, a lone oversized generation counted exactly once, and a config fault deep inside a split still holding the checkpoint.

**Item 5 — `ToolCall.Input` measured, and bounded.** Whole corpus, chronological, 8,552 tool calls:

| metric | bytes |
|---|---|
| min | 0 |
| median | 318 |
| p95 | 2,576 |
| p99 | 8,636 |
| max | 33,411 (`exec`) |
| mean | 737 |

Bounded at **16 KB**, which leaves better than 99% of real tool calls untouched while capping the tail. A cap near p99 would be truncating ordinary traffic.

**The bound is applied at the span, not in `internal/turn`, and that is the decision worth recording.** `internal/turn` is the tempting place, but the same string is also sigil's `tool_call.input_json`, which is *parsed as JSON* rather than displayed. Cutting a JSON document at a byte offset produces something that is not JSON, so truncating at reduce time would silently corrupt the agento11y payload in order to fix a span-attribute problem. `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments` is an opaque display string, so truncation is honest there and nowhere else.

It also cuts on a rune boundary. A span attribute is a UTF-8 string and an exporter handed an invalid one may drop the attribute entirely — trading a large value for no value, which is worse than the problem being fixed. Pinned by a test that puts a 3-byte rune straddling the cut.

`ToolOutput` needs no equivalent: codex-lb truncates it upstream and says so via `ToolOutput.Truncated`. `ToolCall.Input` was the one arriving unbounded.

Items **1** and **2** landed in 4968921 (alongside #12, which shares the same files). All five items are now done, but items 1 and 2 both rested on premises the corpus contradicts, so read this before trusting the issue body.

### Item 1: the tool catalogue is not where this issue says it is

This issue states `response.create` carries `tools[]` with `.name`, `.description`, `.parameters`, `.output_schema` and `.strict`, "**measured present across the full corpus**". Measured again: **zero of 8,916 `response.create` events carry a top-level `tools` key.** `corpus.sig.json`'s own induced signature agrees — the only tool paths under `response.create` are `input[].tools[]` and a nested `input[].tools[].tools[]`. There is no `output_schema` path anywhere.

The real location is an input item of `type: "additional_tools"`, present on **461 of 8,916 creates (5.2%)**, naming 5 top-level entries: `collaboration`, `functions`, `exec`, `wait`, `request_user_input` — some wrapping their own child `tools[]` (`functions` wraps `exec`/`wait`/`request_user_input`, matching the `functions`-namespace note on #3).

Implemented against that, deduped by hash exactly like `InstructionsHash`, with `parameters` and `output_schema` left undecoded — they are client-authored JSON Schema and are precisely why `internal/profile.opaqueKind` exists.

**The consequence worth flagging: `Turn.Tools` will be empty on ~95% of turns, and never contains the model's built-in toolset.** It captures only the dynamically-added set. So sigil's `Generation.tools` will be sparse, and `effective_version` — which the backend derives from `sha256(system_prompt + sorted tools)` — cannot be computed from this capture, because the full catalogue is not on the wire at all. That is a data limitation, not something more code fixes.

### Item 2: `temperature` and `top_p` do not vary

This issue says they "genuinely vary". They do not: **26,691 occurrences each, one distinct value apiece — `temperature` 1.0, `top_p` 0.98.**

The reasoning behind the claim is worth correcting because it will mislead again. The issue inferred variance from those paths carrying no `values` list in `corpus.sig.json`, on the basis that `signature.go` omits `values` above 32 distinct. **That inference cannot hold for a numeric path.** `profile.note` only builds a value histogram for `string` (≤48 chars) and `bool` kinds — a number never gets a `values` list at any cardinality. Absence of `values` on a numeric path carries no information whatsoever.

Both fields are added as specified regardless; they are legitimate request parameters and a future model-config change would show up. But they are constants in this traffic, so they are span/Generation fields only and have no business as metric attributes.

### Pattern across this issue and #12

Four premises in two issues have now been checked against the corpus and three were wrong: `taas_*` (absent or null), the tool catalogue location, `output_schema`'s existence, and `temperature`/`top_p` variance. Plus `engine_total_prompt_tokens_total` being listed as dropped when it was already implemented. Validating before implementing is earning its keep — it is worth budgeting a measurement pass for any issue that asserts a wire fact.
All five items delivered: 3 and 5 in a13a574, 1 and 2 in 4968921. See the comments above for the three corpus corrections to this issue's premises.

body:
## What happened

The full scan behind #20 reported 14 findings. The single most consequential change in that capture was **not one of them**: `request_kind` gained the value `"memory"`, which turned out to be the cause of a silent 4.3x engine-token over-count (see #20 and a052040).

The probe could not have seen it. `x-codex-turn-metadata` is a **JSON document embedded as a string** inside `response.create`'s `client_metadata`. The profiler induces it as a leaf of type `string` and never descends, so every field inside it — `request_kind`, `thread_source`, `subagent_kind`, `sandbox`, `parent_turn_id`, `forked_from_thread_id`, `turn_started_at_unix_ms` — is invisible to drift detection.

Confirmed against the committed baseline: it contains `client_metadata.x-codex-turn-metadata` as a path and nothing beneath it.

## Why it matters more than a coverage gap

This is precisely the block the reducer treats as authoritative. `internal/frame`'s own comment records that reading the *header* copy instead of this one mislabels 89% of turns, and `turn.seriesKey` now depends on `request_kind` for correctness rather than for labelling. So the drift detector is blind to the one document whose contents the pipeline most depends on — and blind in the direction that fails silently, since a new value there changes arithmetic rather than producing an error.

The same shape appears elsewhere: `x-codex-turn-state`, and any other header or field whose value is itself JSON.

## Approach

The profiler needs to know which string-valued paths are embedded documents and recurse into them, rather than guessing by sniffing every string for a leading `{` — sniffing would descend into user prompts and tool output, which is how conversation content ends up in a file whose whole guarantee is that it is content-free.

An explicit, named allowlist keeps that guarantee: a path is treated as an embedded document only if it is listed. `internal/frame` already names these header keys, so the list has an obvious home next to them.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Paths declared as embedded JSON are induced recursively, and appear in `corpus.sig.json` with their own types and value groupings
- [ ] The allowlist is explicit, not sniffed — a prompt body that happens to start with `{` must never be descended into
- [ ] `client_metadata.x-codex-turn-metadata` and the `x-codex-turn-metadata` / `x-codex-turn-state` headers are on it
- [ ] A test proves `request_kind` values appear in the induced signature, so this specific miss cannot recur
- [ ] Baseline regenerated, and any drift the new depth reveals reviewed rather than absorbed
- [ ] Confirm the signature is still content-free after the change — it is the reason the file can be committed at all

Refs #20, #13

comments.body:
Closed by 4d94522.

`request_kind` now reads `[compaction memory prewarm turn]` in the induced signature against the real corpus, at both `client_metadata.x-codex-turn-metadata{}.request_kind` and `header.x-codex-turn-metadata{}.request_kind`. So the specific miss behind #20 cannot recur.

**Mechanism.** Explicit allowlist in a new `internal/profile/embedded.go`, built from `frame.HdrTurnMetadata`/`frame.HdrTurnState` rather than retyped strings. Descended sub-paths use a `{}` marker (`client_metadata.x-codex-turn-metadata{}.request_kind`) — `[]` already means "array element", so `{}` reads as "inside the embedded document" and cannot collide with a real key. Header-embedded documents land in a synthetic `<header>` bucket, following the existing `<payload:kind>` precedent, since headers accompany every record rather than one event type. A value that does not parse as JSON stays a plain string leaf and does not error. `SignatureVersion` 2 → 3, so an old baseline reports "regenerate it" rather than emitting the whole descended path set as drift.

**Two guards had to close before the descent was safe, and only the first was foreseen.**

`code_mode_tool_names` is the client's per-installation tool catalogue, roughly 190 entries, inside an event already sharing its 600-path budget with `tools[].parameters` and `instructions`. Left walked it did more than bury findings the way the unfixed `tools[].parameters` case did — it consumed enough of the cap that **whether `request_kind` survived into the signature depended on Go's map iteration order**, so the corpus test passed or failed at random across runs of identical code. Made opaque, same mechanism as the tool schemas.

**`workspaces` is the serious one, and no test caught it — auditing the generated file did.** It is a map keyed by **absolute filesystem path**, so the key becomes the path segment. The first generated signature contained entries of this shape:

```
workspaces./Users/<user>/repos/<private-repo>.associated_remote_urls.origin
    values = ['<a private git remote>']
workspaces./Users/<user>/repos/<private-repo>.has_changes
```

That is a home directory layout, private repository names, a self-hosted forge hostname and a per-repository dirty flag — in a file that is committed to git specifically because it never carries any of that.

**No existing guard could have stopped it.** `contentSafe` screens *values* by inspecting the name of the segment they sit under, and here the user's data *is* the segment name — there is nothing to screen. `enumValues` screens cardinality, and a handful of repositories passes any cardinality test easily. The only correct fix is to stop the walk before a key is ever turned into a path. Presence and type are still recorded, so `workspaces` appearing, vanishing or changing shape is still a finding.

Separately, `contentSafe` now strips the `{}` marker before testing a segment. Today's three allowlisted paths are all metadata and pass either way, but without the trim, descending into a document at a path like `client_metadata.user` would test the segment as `user{}` — matching neither the denylist nor `identifierish` — and switch the guard off for exactly the document being descended into. Same shape as the `-` versus `_` separator bug already recorded on `identifierish`, and that one reached the baseline before it was caught. Closed before the allowlist grows into it.

**Drift reviewed, not absorbed.** Against the previous baseline: 22 added paths plus the new `<header>` bucket, every one of them embedded descent; zero removed; zero changed types or values on any pre-existing path; storage and record sections byte-identical. Re-scan after regenerating reports no drift, and the committed file contains no filesystem path, host, URL, email or UUID.

Also fixed `clbprobe`'s own usage text, which cost a round of confusion here: it advertised `clbprobe -update corpus/`, which cannot work — `-update` takes the *output* path and the archives are positional.

body:
Full scan of 14 archives / 1,844,497 lines / 4.3GB decompressed, against the committed baseline. **Baseline deliberately NOT regenerated** — these findings are the work.

Found with the probe fixed in 0cada84; the pre-fix full scan reported only 5 of these.

## 1. BREAKING — `response.completed safety_buffering` was bool, now also object

New sub-fields: `.reasons` (array), `.retry_model` (string), `.use_cases` (array of string).

**Already safe.** `internal/turn/reducer.go` decodes it as `json.RawMessage` and `applySafetyBuffering` handles both forms, populating `SafetyBuffering`, `SafetyRetryModel` and `SafetyUseCases`. Verify `.reasons` is captured — it is new and there is no `SafetyReasons` field on `Turn`.

- [x] Confirm no `response.completed` events are being abandoned
- [x] Decide whether `safety_buffering.reasons` is worth a `Turn` field

## 2. The HTTP family has arrived — `request_id` shape `<uuid>`

New: `record.request_id_shape = <uuid>`, plus headers `x-request-id` and `tracestate`.

This is the family that was absent from the camden-only corpus and which `TestReducer_ClassifiesRecordFamilies` could not prove. `frame.Record.Family()` returns `FamilyHTTP` for anything not prefixed `ws_`, so it should classify correctly — but this is the first real data for it.

**The reducer keys on `request_id`.** A UUID request_id is a different id space from `ws_<hex32>`, and #3 records that Postgres `request_id` is the *response* id while the archive's is something else. Check for collisions.

- [x] Corpus test now proves the `http` family (it previously could not)
- [x] Verify reduction over HTTP records produces correct turns, not silently degraded ones
- [x] Confirm `x-request-id` vs archive `request_id` vs `response_id` are not conflated

## 3. New tool: `interrupt_agent`

`response.output_item.added/done item.name = "interrupt_agent"`, and a new `item.status = "completed"`.

- [x] Confirm it flows through `ToolCall` and the `gen_ai.tool.name` cap (64) without becoming `_other`

## 4. Multimodal input — `response.create input[].content[].image_url`

First image content in the capture. The reducer's `captureInput` recovers text parts; an image part is likely dropped or stringified.

- [x] Decide how an image part is represented in `Prompt` and in the Loki content line (do NOT inline base64 — the line budget exists for exactly this)

## 5. `x-openai-subagent = memory_consolidation`

Already seen as a header value; now also inside `response.create client_metadata`.

## Housekeeping

- [x] Regenerate `corpus.sig.json` from a full scan ONLY once each item above is resolved, so nothing is absorbed unreviewed

comments.body:
## Resolved in a052040

Every finding has a verdict. The scan turned up one defect far more serious than anything on the original list.

### The real find: the cumulative baseline was keyed by thread, and a thread runs several counter series at once

`request_kind: "memory"` is not just a new label value. The platform fires memory-consolidation responses **concurrently with the user's turn, on the same `thread_id`**, and each keeps its own logical-turn counter series starting at `num_engine_calls=1`. The reducer kept one baseline per thread, so the response following an interleaved memory response was diffed against the wrong series.

Measured, thread `019fdba7` at 11:06:04:

| | true | reported |
|---|---|---|
| engine prompt tokens delta | 185,287 | **795,246** (4.3x) |
| engine cached tokens delta | 183,296 | **904,192** (4.9x) |
| sampled tokens delta | 606 | **-485** |

12 of 8,078 turns affected. **The token over-count was silent** — the only visible symptom was the negative sampled-token delta, and only because sampled tokens are the one counter where the memory series runs ahead of the turn series.

`TestReducer_NoNegativeDeltas` existed and passed throughout. It read the three cheapest archives; none of the twelve was in them. It now reads the whole corpus (8,113 turns, ~90s) and `TestReducer_InterleavedMemoryKeepsItsOwnBaseline` pins the exact measured numbers synthetically — verified to fail with the old key.

Fix: `seriesKey(t) = thread_id + request_kind`. `State` version 1 -> 2, since v1 keys cannot be migrated (the request_kind half was never recorded) and are discarded rather than reinterpreted.

### 1. safety_buffering

Object form observed twice, both `{"use_cases":["bio"],"reasons":[],"retry_model":"gpt-5.6-luna"}`. Decoding was already safe; **zero** `response.completed` events abandoned across 1.84M records. `SafetyReasons` added — carried on the strength of what it means (the only field that explains rather than describes) rather than of what it has so far contained, which is nothing.

### 2. HTTP family

**Real, and correctly classified.** `x-codex-turn-state` is `http_turn_`-prefixed as the doc claimed, and `x-request-id` + `tracestate` are present on 100% of them and 0% of websocket records.

- **No id-space collision.** 73 distinct UUID ids vs 887 `ws_` ids, disjoint, asserted rather than assumed. Zero threads mix the two shapes.
- **No degradation.** 75 HTTP turns, 69 completed, 0 missing a model, 0 completed without tokens.
- **`x-request-id` is NOT the record's `request_id`.** They agree on 5,685 of 22,837 records and disagree on 17,152 — the header is connection-scoped and goes stale exactly like `x-codex-turn-metadata`. Recorded on `HdrRequestID`.
- One correction: these records still carry `transport: websocket` and a `wss://` URL, because the archive captures codex-lb's **upstream** connection, which is a websocket whatever the client used. The family describes the client's request mode and nothing on the record's transport fields reveals it.

**Bug found here**: an empty `request_id` was classified `FamilyHTTP`, because the test was "not prefixed `ws_`". Those are the connection-level close and error frames — so a websocket dying was booked as an HTTP-family error, in exactly the records that exist to report a connection dying. 7 turns mislabelled. Now `FamilyUnknown`.

### 3. interrupt_agent

Flows through fine. Nine distinct tool names across the whole corpus against a cap of 64: `exec`, `spawn_agent`, `wait_agent`, `list_agents`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `interrupt_agent`, `request_user_input`, `wait`. Nothing collapses to `_other`. `Observed` updated to the measured set (it listed `functions`, which is not in this corpus).

### 4. Multimodal input

3 image parts, all `type: input_image`, `image_url` a `data:image/png;base64,…` URI **up to 784 KB**.

The failure was the opposite of the feared one: `flattenText` finds no `text` field on an image part, so an image-only message flattened to `""` and was dropped whole, leaving no trace an image was ever sent. No base64 was ever at risk of reaching Loki — but nothing recorded the image either.

Now counted and never carried (`Turn.InputImages`, `Prompt.Images`). A test asserts no prompt text contains `data:image` or `;base64,`, because a Loki line over the limit is discarded whole rather than truncated — one inlined screenshot would destroy the user message it belongs to.

### 5. memory_consolidation

7 occurrences as `x-openai-subagent` in `client_metadata`; already handled into `SubagentKind`. Added to `Observed` along with `collab_spawn` and `thread_spawn`. Distinct from the `request_kind: "memory"` above — different field, different records.

### Housekeeping

`corpus.sig.json` regenerated from a full scan **after** every item had a verdict. Re-scan reports no drift. `TestReducer_RequestKindsAreNamed` now fails on any request kind the corpus contains that `internal/frame` does not name, since an unnamed kind is a counter series being diffed against the wrong baseline rather than a mere labelling gap.

Follow-up filed as #21: the probe could not have caught the most consequential value in this scan.
Closed by a052040. Every checkbox verified against the full corpus rather than assumed; see the resolution comment above. Follow-up in #21.
