body:
## Why

Grafana's agent-observability app (sigil) would give us a conversation-shaped view of codex-lb traffic for free. Two source repos read for this: `/Users/<user>/repos/sigil` (the app) and `/Users/<user>/repos/sigil-sdk` (the in-process instrumentation SDK).

## The finding that reshapes this: sigil is not a trace viewer

Its product surface — conversations, generations, agent catalog, eval filters — is populated **only** by `GenerationIngestService.ExportGenerations`, or by an OTLP *traces* receiver that decodes specially-shaped spans back into `sigil.v1.Generation`. Forwarding spans to a trace backend is an explicit non-goal in its own design doc. Plain OTLP traces to a generic collector land in Tempo and **nowhere in sigil's database**.

It also has **no OTLP metrics receiver at all** — our entire metrics sink is irrelevant to agento11y visibility.

The decoder works **per span**, not per trace. Each qualifying span becomes one `Generation`; a parent and its child both describing the same inference is a known double-count in that model.

### Gate for the tolerant generic path

- `gen_ai.operation.name` ∈ {`chat`, `generate_content`, `text_completion`, `invoke_agent`} — **the discriminator**
- `gen_ai.provider.name` and `gen_ai.request.model` (or `response.model`); both may be omitted only for `invoke_agent`
- non-zero trace and span ids

A span failing this is skipped and reported as OTLP `partial_success` — **never an error**, so an exporter goes on reporting success while nothing lands. This is the same failure shape as the Loki 204.

**As of 228c717 our `chat <model>` span passes this gate.** `gen_ai.conversation.id` is already `ThreadID`, so conversation grouping works; `gen_ai.agent.name` falls back to resource `service.name`.

## Can we use the SDK directly?

**Not its high-level API.** `Client.StartGeneration`/`End` creates a live OTel span and `applyTraceContextFromSpan` unconditionally overwrites the trace and span ids with the SDK's own generated ones, so our deterministic archive-derived ids never survive. Historical timestamps ARE honoured (`GenerationStart.StartedAt` / `Generation.CompletedAt`), and `Generation.ID` is caller-settable — it is specifically trace identity that is lost.

**There is a usable lower path**: `codec.ToProto(model.Generation)` is exported, takes a hand-built Generation with caller-chosen `ID`, `TraceID`, `SpanID`, `StartedAt`, `CompletedAt`, and involves no span, tracer or live call. Paired with the generated gRPC/HTTP client this is a legitimate backfill path — but it means writing our own emitter against sigil's wire contract, which is what `internal/sink/otlptrace` already does for Tempo.

**So the cheap route is: shape the existing span to the wire contract and point it at sigil's receiver.** Not reimplement the SDK.

## Coverage from a passive capture

Roughly **55-65% of the Generation signal** — the one that actually drives the UI — and much lower outside it.

**Already emitted or 1:1:** conversation id, operation name, provider, request/response model, response id, all six token counts, started/completed, error detail, trace/span ids.

**Derivable with real work:** system prompt (emitted once per hash as a separate line — needs a join), input messages (`Turn.Prompts`), output messages (`Turn.Messages` + `ToolCalls`), parent generation ids (`ParentTurnID`/`ParentThreadID`, needs id-space translation), `mode` STREAM vs SYNC (`TextDeltaCount > 0`), `effective_version` (`InstructionsHash`).

**Tool catalogue — CORRECTION to the research brief.** It was reported as "likely present, unverified". It is **measured**: `corpus.sig.json` records `response.tools[].name`, `.description`, `.parameters`, `.output_schema` and `.strict` across the full corpus. The data is definitely there; `internal/turn`'s `createEvent` simply does not decode it (only `parallel_tool_calls`). This is reducer work, not a discovery problem.

**Permanent gaps that would visibly degrade the app, in priority order:**
1. **Per-tool-call latency does not exist in the capture.** Every tool-call span currently spans the full response duration — an acknowledged approximation. Any sigil view splitting time-in-tool from time-in-model would be systematically *wrong*, not merely absent. Worst item on this list.
2. **Token usage is metric-only**, so a decoded generation has `Usage = nil` — no tokens, no cost. Covered by #18.
3. **Tool schema catalogue** not reduced — any "tools available to this agent" surface is empty until the reducer work above.
4. **User and agent identity.** No agent-name concept exists; `SafetyID` is the only user-ish value and is deliberately `Sensitive`, excluded from metrics, labels and spans. Per-user filtering and agent-catalog rows will be sparse.
5. **`stop_reason` granularity** — our four statuses are coarser than the finish-reason vocabulary, and `transport` has no equivalent.

**Flatly impossible, and worth recording so nobody re-investigates:** conversation title, freeform tags/metadata, guardrail hook verdicts, human conversation ratings, embeddings (no such calls in this capture), and general `WorkflowStep` — that models the harness's internal decision graph, which never crosses the websocket. codex-lb sees model-call boundaries only.

## Scope

- [ ] Confirm the deployment question this code read cannot settle: sigil listens on its **own** OTLP endpoint, distinct from Grafana Cloud's gateway. Establish whether an agento11y instance is reachable at all before building anything.
- [ ] Decide the route: reshape existing spans for the OTLP receiver (cheap, already 90% there) vs a native `ExportGenerations` sink via `codec.ToProto` (full fidelity, own wire contract).
- [ ] Token usage on spans (blocked on #18).
- [ ] Reduce the tool catalogue from `response.create` into `Turn`.
- [ ] Content parts: map `Turn.Prompts`/`Messages`/`ToolCalls`/`ToolOutputs` onto the input/output message model, subject to the same truncation limits the Loki path already has.
- [ ] Record per-tool-call timing as a known unfixable approximation wherever it surfaces, rather than letting it read as a measurement.

Depends on #18. Blocked on the endpoint question above.

comments.body:
**Unblocked.** There are two endpoints, not one:

- Generic OTLP for traces and metrics: `https://otlp-gateway-prod-gb-south-1.grafana.net/otlp`
- agento11y / sigil for conversation data: `https://agento11y-prod-gb-south-1.grafana.net`

Instance `<GRAFANA_STACK_ID>`, and **the same credentials already used for traces and logs** — no new token needed. So sigil support is additive: keep the existing OTLP trace path as-is and add a second emitter for the Generation wire contract, rather than re-pointing anything.

## Seam frozen — route decided, wire shape measured

Read out of `/Users/<user>/repos/sigil-sdk`, not inferred.

**Route (checkbox 2): native `ExportGenerations` over HTTP+JSON.** Not reshaped OTLP spans. The agento11y endpoint speaks the sigil Generation protocol; the existing OTLP trace path to Tempo stays exactly as it is and nothing is re-pointed. This is purely additive.

**Transport:**
- `POST https://agento11y-prod-gb-south-1.grafana.net/api/v1/generations:export`
- `Content-Type: application/json`, body is protojson of `ExportGenerationsRequest` with `UseProtoNames: true`
- `Authorization: Basic base64(user:token)` — instance `<GRAFANA_STACK_ID>`, the same credentials already used for Loki and OTLP
- Proto source of truth: `proto/agento11y/v1/generation_ingest.proto`

**The exact JSON, produced by running the SDK's own marshaller rather than reading the proto and hoping:**

```json
{"generations":[{"id":"gen-1","conversation_id":"thread-1","operation_name":"chat",
"mode":"GENERATION_MODE_STREAM","trace_id":"0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c",
"span_id":"b7ad6b7169203331","model":{"provider":"openai","name":"gpt-5.6-sol"},
"response_id":"resp_x","response_model":"gpt-5.6-sol",
"input":[{"role":"MESSAGE_ROLE_USER","parts":[{"text":"hi"},
{"media":{"kind":"image","mime_type":"image/png"}}]}],
"usage":{"input_tokens":"10","output_tokens":"2","total_tokens":"12",
"input_semantics":"TOKEN_INPUT_SEMANTICS_INCLUSIVE"},
"started_at":"2026-08-07T13:32:33Z","completed_at":"2026-08-07T13:32:39Z",
"tags":{"codexlb.family":"websocket"}}]}
```

Four encoding traps, each of which a hand-written Go struct gets wrong by default:

1. **int64 fields marshal as JSON STRINGS** — `"input_tokens":"10"`, not `10`. Every `TokenUsage` field is int64.
2. **Enums are full symbolic names** — `GENERATION_MODE_STREAM`, `MESSAGE_ROLE_USER`, `TOKEN_INPUT_SEMANTICS_INCLUSIVE`.
3. Timestamps are RFC3339 strings.
4. Zero-valued fields are omitted entirely.

Tag map keys keep their dots. `attr.LokiKey` is a Loki-only concern and must not be applied here.

**A 200 is not proof of delivery.** `ExportGenerationsResponse` carries `results[]` with a per-generation `accepted` bool and `error` string. This is the third instance of that shape in this project — Loki returns 204 for lines it discards, and sigil's OTLP receiver reports `partial_success` rather than an error. The sink reads `results[].accepted` and counts rejections per generation.

**Dependency `github.com/grafana/agento11y/go v0.16.0` added in d05c1b9, for a TEST ONLY.** The emitter is hand-written, like the Loki one, so no protobuf or grpc is linked into the binary. The dependency exists so a conformance test can decode our hand-built JSON with the SDK's own generated types — turning "the shape looks right" into proof.

**`effective_version` trap:** the proto requires `^sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}$` and ingest rejects anything else. Our `InstructionsHash` is a *truncated* sha256 (16 hex chars, `turn.shortHash`), so it does not qualify and cannot simply be passed through.

**Descoped from this pass**, tracked but not attempted: the tool catalogue (`response.tools[]` -> `ToolDefinition`, needs reducer work), per-tool-call latency (does not exist in the capture — left unset rather than emitted as an approximation that would read as a measurement), and `WorkflowStep` ingest.

**Images**: emitted as a `Media` part with `kind`/`mime_type` and no url. The payload is deliberately not retained (base64 data URIs up to 784 KB) and must never be reconstructed — see #20.

## Closed by d4cfe31

`internal/sink/agento11y` is a fourth sink, additive — the OTLP trace path to Tempo is unchanged and nothing was re-pointed. Enabled with `agento11y.enabled: true`, off by default.

**The conformance test is the load-bearing one.** The emitter is hand-written against sigil's JSON, so no protobuf or grpc is linked into the binary; the SDK is a test dependency whose whole job is to decode our hand-built JSON with the real generated types. That turns "the shape looks right" into proof, and it caught all four protojson traps that a Go struct gets wrong by default.

**A 200 is not delivery.** `results[]` is parsed on every 2xx, `accepted:false` is counted, and a generation that comes back with *no verdict at all* counts as rejected rather than assumed. Third time this project has met that shape after Loki's 204 and sigil's OTLP `partial_success`.

**One defect found in review: 413 had to be a DATA fault.** Every other permanent 4xx holds the checkpoint, so a misconfiguration surfaces rather than running forever delivering nothing. But a batch too large to accept is too large on every retry, so holding the checkpoint there wedges the pipeline on a batch that can never drain — the same failure from the opposite direction. Reachable, not theoretical: a batch is 200 generations carrying prompts up to 32 KB each. Counted and dropped, with halve-and-retry filed as #22.

**Images now carry their declared media type.** The reducer reads it from the data URI's own declaration in the first 30 bytes, before the base64 begins — never sniffed from the payload, so it stays bounded, and absent rather than guessed when the URI declares nothing. Payload still never carried; `url` stays empty because the only url these ever had *was* the payload, inline.

### Deliberate omissions, each pinned by a test so a future change is a decision rather than a side effect

- **`stop_reason`** — unset, for the same reason `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons` is on #18. The two must agree or the codebase holds two answers to one question. `codexlb.status` already rides in tags under a name that means what it says.
- **`effective_version`** — the proto rejects anything but `^sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}$`, and `InstructionsHash` is truncated to 16 hex chars. Prefixing `sha256:` would satisfy the regex while lying about being a sum of anything. Relying on the documented server-side fallback.
- **`parent_generation_ids`** — `ParentTurnID` is in the server's `turn_*` space, `Generation.id` in the `resp_*` space, with no local join short of caching every mapping the process has seen. An id that resolves to nothing is worse than an absent field.
- **Per-tool-call latency** — does not exist in the capture. Left unset rather than emitted as an approximation that would read as a measurement. This was the worst item on the original coverage list and it remains a permanent gap.
- **Tool catalogue** — needs reducer work; filed as #22 along with `AgentMessages` and the `temperature`/`top_p` reduction.

### Checkbox 1, retrospectively

The deployment question is settled: reachable, same credentials, instance `<GRAFANA_STACK_ID>`. Nothing has been pushed to it — deployment waits on #10 per the standing constraint.

## Enabled on camden

`c06983e`. The sink has been fully wired since this issue closed, but `config.example.yaml` had no `agento11y:` section at all - so the only way to turn it on was to already know the field names from the source. Added, `enabled: true`, and installed on camden.

`agento11y-prod-gb-south-1.grafana.net` resolves to `k8s-sigilpro-sigilpro-...elb.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com`, so the region default is right for instance <GRAFANA_STACK_ID>. `/opt/codexlb2otel/.env` already carried `CODEXLB2OTEL_AGENTO11Y_TOKEN`. `config.Load` (which runs `Validate`) accepts the section against the real image.

Additive to the OTLP trace export, as designed - `buildSinks` appends it alongside `otlptrace`, it does not replace it.

Not yet exercised against the live endpoint: the service is not started. The thing to check on first run is the **per-generation** verdicts in the response body, not the HTTP status - `accountResults` parses them precisely because a 2xx here can still refuse individual generations.

title: Grafana sigil / agento11y support: emit Generations, not just traces

body:
## Why

#3 froze the naming rule as "`gen_ai.*` where the convention defines the concept, `codexlb.*` where it does not". The second half was applied too widely. Diffing our contract against the 60 distinct `gen_ai.*` attributes Grafana's own agent SDK uses (`/Users/<user>/repos/sigil-sdk`) shows several things we invented a name for **do** have a standard one.

That matters beyond tidiness: anything consuming the convention — dashboards, Grafana's agent-observability app, any future correlation with `genai-otel-bridge` — keys on the standard spelling and finds nothing from us.

Already fixed separately in 228c717: no span carried `gen_ai.operation.name` or `gen_ai.provider.name` at all, which made every span invisible to a convention-aware consumer.

## Renames — we have the data, under the wrong name

| standard | ours today | source |
|---|---|---|
| `gen_ai.tool.name` | `codexlb.tool_name` | `ToolCall.Name` |
| `gen_ai.client.time_to_first_token` | `codexlb.time_to_first_token` | `Turn.TTFTMs` |
| `gen_ai.usage.server_tool_use.web_search_requests` | `codexlb.web_search_requests` | `Turn.WebSearchRequests` |
| `gen_ai.request.thinking.level` | `codexlb.reasoning_effort` | `Turn.Effort` |
| `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons` | `codexlb.status` | `Turn.Status` (see caveat) |

`codexlb.status` is the awkward one. Our four values (`completed`/`incomplete`/`transport`/`error`) are a coarser classification than the convention's finish-reason vocabulary, and `transport` has no equivalent at all. Options: emit both, emit `finish_reasons` only where it genuinely maps, or keep ours and document the divergence. **Decide before renaming** — a standard name carrying non-standard values is worse than a clearly non-standard name.

## Additions — data we have and do not currently emit as attributes

- `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `total_tokens`, `reasoning_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`, `cache_write_input_tokens` — all six exist on `Turn`. Today they are only a counter split by `gen_ai.token.type`, so **a decoded generation has no usage at all** and no cost or token figures anywhere a span is the unit.
- `gen_ai.tool.call.id`, `gen_ai.tool.type`, `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments`, `gen_ai.tool.call.result` — `ToolCall.CallID`, `.Kind`, `.Input`, and `ToolOutput.Text`. Currently sink-local or unemitted.
- `gen_ai.client.tool_calls_per_operation` — `len(Turn.ToolCalls)`.
- `gen_ai.operation.name` should be `execute_tool` on tool spans and `invoke_agent` on subagent spans, not `chat` everywhere. Note the double-count trap fixed in 228c717: exactly one span per response may claim to be the inference.

## Explicitly NOT applicable

`gen_ai.embeddings.*` (no embedding calls in this capture), `gen_ai.evaluation.*` (no evaluations), `gen_ai.request.max_tokens`/`temperature`/`top_p` (not on the wire — checked, `createEvent` carries no such field).

## Standing deviation, re-affirmed

`gen_ai.client.token.usage` is specified as a **histogram**; we emit counters under `codexlb.*`. That deviation stays — the question is "tokens by model and account", which is a sum. But a parallel histogram under the standard name is cheap and makes us visible to anything querying the convention. Worth doing rather than choosing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each rename above applied or explicitly rejected with a reason recorded here
- [ ] `codexlb.status` vs `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons` decided before any rename lands
- [ ] Token usage available as span attributes, not only as a counter
- [ ] Tool spans carry `gen_ai.tool.*` and `gen_ai.operation.name=execute_tool`
- [ ] Subagent spans carry `gen_ai.operation.name=invoke_agent`
- [ ] Parallel `gen_ai.client.token.usage` histogram alongside the counter
- [ ] A test asserts every `codexlb.*` key we keep has no standard equivalent, so this cannot drift back

Refs #3, #7, #11

comments.body:
## Blocking decision resolved: `codexlb.status` stays, `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons` is NOT emitted

The issue said to decide this before any rename lands. Decided on measurement, from the full-corpus signature (`corpus.sig.json`, 1.84M records):

| path | finding |
|---|---|
| `response.status` | exactly **one** value ever: `"completed"` |
| `response.incomplete_details` | always `null` |
| `finish_reason` | **absent from the capture entirely** |
| `stop_reason` | **absent from the capture entirely** |

So there is no finish-reason data on the wire at all. Three of our four status values — `incomplete`, `transport`, `error` — are produced by *this service*, not the server, and the fourth is a constant.

**This corrects the issue's own framing.** It said our values are "a coarser classification than the convention's finish-reason vocabulary". They are not coarser, they are a **different axis**: `codexlb.status` answers "did our pipeline observe this response finish", which is a pipeline-health question, not a model-behaviour question. `completed` is not `stop` — we never learn whether generation ended on a stop token or on a length limit.

Emitting the standard name would make a convention-aware dashboard display a fabricated finish reason instead of an honest gap, which is worse than a clearly non-standard name. The divergence is recorded on the `Status` constant rather than left as a silent omission.

## Second correction: temperature and top_p ARE on the wire

The issue states `gen_ai.request.max_tokens`/`temperature`/`top_p` are "not on the wire — checked, `createEvent` carries no such field". That is right about `createEvent` and **wrong about the wire**. They are on `response.completed`:

- `response.temperature` — number, present
- `response.top_p` — number, present
- `response.max_output_tokens` — null, so that one genuinely is absent

Whether they are worth emitting depends on whether they vary, which is being checked rather than assumed.

## Frozen for implementation

Renames, with the attribute/metric distinction the issue's table conflated:

| kind | from | to |
|---|---|---|
| attribute | `codexlb.tool_name` | `gen_ai.tool.name` |
| attribute | `codexlb.reasoning_effort` | `gen_ai.request.thinking.level` |
| **metric** | `codexlb.time_to_first_token` | `gen_ai.client.time_to_first_token` |
| **metric** | `codexlb.web_search_requests` | convention's server-tool-use name |

Plus: token usage as span attributes, `gen_ai.tool.*` on tool spans, `gen_ai.operation.name` = `execute_tool` / `invoke_agent` on the right spans, and a parallel `gen_ai.client.token.usage` histogram beside the counter.

Standing trap, re-affirmed: **exactly one span per response may declare itself a GenAI inference.** 228c717 added `gen_ai.operation.name`/`provider.name` to the chat span only, deliberately not via `SpanAttrs`, because that would make the turn root and every child claim to be an inference and consumers would count the turn several times.

## Closed by 954bd03 — with three corrections to this issue's own rename table

**The table above named three attributes that do not exist.** It was written against the pre-move shape of the conventions. Verified against `open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai@main`, `model/gen-ai/{registry,metrics}.yaml`, 2026-08-07:

| this issue said | reality |
|---|---|
| `gen_ai.request.thinking.level` | **does not exist**. The real name is `gen_ai.request.reasoning.level` (`registry.yaml:171` — its own brief reads "The reasoning or thinking effort level", so the concept was right and the key was not) |
| `gen_ai.client.time_to_first_token` | **does not exist**. The real name is `gen_ai.server.time_to_first_token` (`metrics.yaml:111`) |
| `gen_ai.usage.server_tool_use.web_search_requests` | **no such concept anywhere** in the registry, the metrics, or `docs/gen-ai/openai.md` |

So `codexlb.web_search_requests` **keeps its name**. There is nothing to line it up with, and a plausible-looking standard name that no consumer actually defines is worse than an honestly local one.

`server.` over `client.` is a semantic choice, not a namespace preference: the metric is defined as "Time to generate first token for successful responses", and ours comes from the server's own `first_sampled_message_ttft_ms`. The client-side sibling `gen_ai.client.operation.time_to_first_chunk` measures from when the client issued the request, which this capture never sees.

The table also conflated attributes with metric instrument names — two of the four renames are metrics.

**Token spellings differed too.** The issue listed `cache_write_input_tokens` and `total_tokens`; the spec has `gen_ai.usage.cache_creation.input_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.reasoning.output_tokens`, and **no** `gen_ai.usage.total_tokens` at all.

## Bug found and fixed on the way

`Guard.With` had no Sensitive-class filter. `SpanAttrs`, `MetricAttrs` and `Labels` enforce the class by walking the registry and skipping Sensitive; `With` takes an arbitrary caller-supplied key and would have capped-and-forwarded a Sensitive one straight past all three — the one available path to putting `safety_identifier` on a span, which Tempo indexes for search. Nothing used it. Closed anyway, plus a registry invariant that rejects a Sensitive caller-supplied field at registration rather than trusting every call site.

## Deferred, and why

`temperature` and `top_p` are on the wire (correcting this issue's "not on the wire — checked"), and they genuinely vary rather than being constants. But `turn.Turn` carries neither field, so emitting them is reducer work rather than an attribute rename. Filed as #22.

Double-count trap from 228c717 verified intact: exactly one span still declares `chat`. `execute_tool` and `invoke_agent` describe the tool call, not the inference, so they do not compete for it.

title: GenAI semconv compliance: several codexlb.* names have standard equivalents

body:
Turned up while fixing #16. The archive carries websocket connection-health signals that no planned metric covers, and they are exactly the kind of thing that is invisible in codex-lb's own UI.

## What exists in the corpus

**Control frames.** 20 across 1,495,378 lines. `internal/frame` models them (`Extra.FrameType`, `Extra.CloseCode`) and `internal/turn/reducer.go` folds `close_code` into the turn, so the data is already reaching the reducer — it just has nowhere to go yet.

| count | frame_type | close_code | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18 | `error` | `null` | `no close frame received or sent` — connection dropped without a close handshake |
| 1 | `error` | `1012` | `received 1012 (service restart); then sent 1012` — OpenAI restarted a backend |
| 1 | `close` | `1000` | clean close |

**Connection-limit errors.** New as of 2026-08-07, one occurrence so far:

```json
{"type":"error","status":400,"error":{
  "type":"invalid_request_error",
  "code":"websocket_connection_limit_reached",
  "message":"Responses websocket connection limit reached (60 minutes). Create a new websocket connection to continue."}}
```

This is an OpenAI-side ceiling the traffic is now hitting. It is a `text` frame carrying a protocol `error` event, so it is a different mechanism from the control frames above and needs its own handling.

## Why it matters

An unclean disconnect and a service restart both look like latency or a failed turn from every angle currently planned. Without close-code attribution, "the turn failed" and "OpenAI restarted the backend under us" are indistinguishable — and the second one is not a codex-lb problem at all. The connection-limit error is worse: it is a capacity ceiling that will get more frequent as usage grows, and it has a documented remedy (reconnect at 60 minutes), so it is exactly the thing an alert should catch early.

## Scope

- [ ] Counter for websocket closes, attributed by `close_code` and `frame_type`
- [ ] Counter for protocol `error` events attributed by `error.code`, with `websocket_connection_limit_reached` called out
- [ ] Decide whether an unclean disconnect (`close_code: null`) should mark the in-flight turn as incomplete rather than leaving it looking like a normal turn that simply stopped
- [ ] Alert on connection-limit errors — a rising rate means codex-lb needs to recycle connections sooner
- [ ] Cardinality check: `close_code` is a small integer set and `error.code` is a server-side enum, so both are safe as attributes, but pin that with the probe's enum histogram rather than assuming it

Depends on #3 (attribute contract) and #7 (OTLP metrics). Alerting belongs with #14.

comments.body:
Closed by 7f57ff8. Validated before implementing, as most of this was already reaching the reducer and the attribute registry — `codexlb.close_code` and `codexlb.frame_type` are both in `internal/attr` with measured caps, and the full-corpus cap test (added on #3 in the same commit) confirms `close_code ∈ {1000, 1012}` and `frame_type ∈ {close, error}`.

The gap was the transport counter, in two ways, and the second is the one that mattered:

**It under-counted.** The condition was `Status == transport || CloseCode != nil`. `StatusTransport` is set only on the *uncorrelated* path (`addUncorrelated`), so an error frame that arrived correlated to an in-flight request — no close code, turn ends `incomplete` — was counted **nowhere at all**. The corpus splits 13 uncorrelated / 7 correlated, so this was not a corner case. Now also triggered by `FrameErrors > 0`.

**It was unreadable.** It carried `close_code` but not `frame_type`. 18 of the 20 transport events are an error frame with *no* close code, so attributed by `close_code` alone they collapse into one bucket whose only distinguishing feature is an absent attribute — which reads on a dashboard as missing data rather than as a connection that died without a handshake. `frame_type` is the axis separating "OpenAI restarted the backend under us" (1012) from "the connection dropped" from a clean 1000, and those want different runbooks.

Pinned by `TestTransportEvents_UncleanDropIsCountedAndDistinguishable`, three cases, verified to fail on both halves without the change.

**Scope items, as settled:**

- [x] Counter for closes attributed by `close_code` and `frame_type` — `codexlb.transport_events{family, account_id, close_code, frame_type}`
- [x] Counter for protocol `error` events by `error.code` — `codexlb.errors` already carries `error.type` + `codexlb.error_code`; the corpus confirms `websocket_connection_limit_reached` arrives as a value there
- [x] **Decision: an unclean disconnect already marks the turn `incomplete`, and that is correct.** No change needed. A correlated transport frame does not set a terminal status, so the turn never sees `response.completed` and `flush.go` gives it `incomplete` — which is honest: the pipeline genuinely does not know whether the model finished. The transport counter now carries the *reason* alongside it, so `incomplete` + `frame_type=error` is attributable rather than looking like a turn that simply stopped.
- [x] Cardinality check pinned by the probe/corpus rather than assumed — `close_code` 2/32, `error_code` 2/64, `frame_type` 2/8 over 1.84M lines
- [ ] **Alerting deferred to #14**, as this issue's own last line says. Carried over there.

title: Surface websocket connection health: control frames and connection-limit errors

body:
Found while working out why a sampled scan and a full scan disagreed. (They did not — the corpus grew between the two runs. But investigating turned up three real defects in the probe itself.)

## 1. Websocket control frames are classified as a transport change

`payload.text` on a control frame is a human-readable close reason, not a protocol event:

| count | frame_type | close_code | payload.text |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18 | `error` | `null` | `no close frame received or sent` |
| 1 | `error` | `1012` | `received 1012 (service restart); then sent 1012 (service restart)` |
| 1 | `close` | `1000` | *(empty)* |

That is every non-`text` frame in 1,495,378 lines. Feeding them to `framing()` yields `plain-text` and `empty`, and `Diff` grades a new framing bucket as BREAKING with "an SSE or chunked transport would look like this" — a standing false alarm about a transport that does not exist. It also inflates `payload_text_not_json`, which reads as damaged data.

`internal/frame` already models these correctly (`frame.go:78-79`, `frame.go:176`) and `internal/turn/reducer.go:175-178` folds them into the turn, so nothing was ever being dropped. The bug is entirely in the profiler's classification.

**Fix:** exclude any record whose `extra.frame_type` is non-empty and not `text` from `PayloadFraming` and `PayloadUnparsed`; count them separately as `TransportFrames`. Tested by exclusion rather than against a list of known control types, so an unseen control frame is classified correctly on first appearance while still surfacing as a new `extra.frame_type` enum value.

## 2. A field turning nullable is graded BREAKING

`Diff` grades any added type as BREAKING (`signature.go`), on the reasoning that a typed Go decoder abandons the whole event on a mismatch. True for `string`↔`array` — that is the bug that silently discarded 1,500 input items — but **not** for `null`: `encoding/json` accepts null into any Go type as a no-op and leaves the zero value, so no data is lost.

Three real cases were affected (`codex.rate_limits` `rate_limits`, `additional_rate_limits`, `credits.balance`). Spending the top severity on changes that destroy nothing is how BREAKING stops being read.

**Fix:** null additions become `NEW` under a new kind `event.path.nullable`. Pinned by a test that also asserts the contrasting type-mismatch case still errors, so the justification is not left on trust.

## 3. `-json` is not machine-readable

The human shape summary prints to stdout ahead of the JSON document, so `clbprobe -json ... | jq` fails on line 1. Hit this while checking the numbers for this issue.

**Fix:** under `-json` the summary goes to stderr. A human still sees it; stdout is a clean document.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Control frames excluded from framing and unparsed counts, reported on their own line
- [ ] `null` type additions graded NEW, not BREAKING
- [ ] `-json` writes only JSON to stdout
- [ ] Tests for all three, including the `encoding/json` null behaviour the grading depends on
- [ ] Baseline regenerated from a full scan and committed

## Note on the baseline

`corpus.sig.json` had an uncommitted regeneration in the working tree that silently absorbed the three null additions above, 66 new paths (the memory-consolidation `text.format` schema), the `x-openai-memgen-request` header and `x-openai-subagent: memory_consolidation`. Reviewed, and rolled into the regeneration here.

Also worth its own issue: `websocket_connection_limit_reached` now appears in the corpus — `Responses websocket connection limit reached (60 minutes). Create a new websocket connection to continue.`, status 400. That is an OpenAI-side ceiling the traffic is hitting, and a candidate metric.

Full scan is clean; the sampled scan exits 0 with 0 breaking, 0 new. `clbprobe -json` pipes into `jq` without a filter. All 8 packages green, gofmt and vet clean.

title: clbprobe: three defects found while explaining a false BREAKING finding

body:
## The query this project exists to serve

Given a response id copied out of codex-lb's UI, a dashboard or an alert, answer in Grafana:

- **why did this call use this model and these thinking parameters?**
- **what was actually said during the conversation?**

Neither is answerable today. codex-lb's UI shows the model and effort per request and will show the
raw archive payloads, but reconstructing the conversation from them is impractical - the response
above is 337 frames, and the conversation it belongs to is 309 responses.

`cmd/clbfind` (014b04b) already does this offline against the corpus and is the working prototype of
the output. This issue is making the same thing work in Grafana against live data.

## The id trap - resolve this in #3

codex-lb's UI labels `resp_*` as **"Request ID"**. The archive's own `request_id` is something else
entirely. All four ids are distinct and all four are things somebody will paste into a query box:

| what you paste | what it is | where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| `resp_052b6a...118909` | OpenAI response id | `request_logs.request_id`, archive `response.id` |
| `ws_481fa8fa...48ce` | archive request id | `request_logs.archive_request_id`, archive `request_id` |
| `019fdb99-a66a-...` | thread / conversation | `request_logs.conversation_id`, archive `thread_id` |
| `019fdb97-294e-...` | session | `session_id` in both |

A lookup that only indexes one of these fails whenever somebody pastes another. All four must be
queryable structured metadata on the Loki side.

## Scope

- Every emitted record carries all four ids as structured metadata, so one Loki query by any of them
  returns the turn.
- A turn record carries the *why*: model, reasoning effort, verbosity, service tier, reasoning
  context/mode - plus the routing metadata that explains them, which is the part codex-lb's UI cannot
  show. `thread_source=subagent`, `subagent_kind`, `parent_thread_id` and `forked_from_thread_id`
  are what turn "it used xhigh" into "it used xhigh because it is a spawned subagent of thread X".
- **Content lines carry the thread id**, so filtering by thread reconstructs the conversation in
  order. One response is rarely the answer: a mid-turn continuation carries only the tool result that
  provoked it, and the human's request is many responses back.
- `previous_response_id` emitted so the response chain can be walked.
- A Grafana dashboard with a response-id / thread-id variable that lands on: the metadata panel, the
  timing breakdown, and the conversation in order. Belongs with #14.

## Worked example, for the acceptance test

`resp_052b6a1e90eb18d3016a75b032be90819198bd170a3e118909` (2026-08-07T10, in the corpus):

```
model gpt-5.6-sol, effort xhigh, verbosity low, service tier default
request_kind turn, thread_source subagent, subagent_kind thread_spawn
parent_thread_id 019fdb97-294e-7d52-af76-399e39413bce  <- the why
elapsed 13.0s, ttft 1219ms, engine wall 12481ms, pre-inference 254ms
208010 in (203520 cached, ratio 0.978) / 490 out / 153 reasoning
337 frames; thread 019fdb99-a66a-7841-a420-e9f8602d4034 holds 309 responses
```

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All four ids are queryable structured metadata on every emitted record.
- [ ] A single Loki query by response id returns the turn's metadata and its content.
- [ ] A single query by thread id returns the conversation in order.
- [ ] The routing fields that explain the parameters are present on every turn.
- [ ] Dashboard variable accepts any of the four ids.
- [ ] Verified against the worked example above, matching `clbfind` output field for field.

Depends on #3 (the id naming must be settled there) and #5. Dashboard work is #14.

comments.body:
## Validated against the code before implementing. Most of this was already true.

The "id trap" half of this issue — the part it was mainly filed for — was already solved by the Loki sink's architecture, not by anything added for it. `buildLines` computes one `baseMeta` from `attr.Guard.Metadata` per `Turn` and reuses it unmodified for **every** record type, so all four ids ride on every line by construction rather than by each record type remembering to include them.

| criterion | verdict |
|---|---|
| All four ids as structured metadata on every record | **already satisfied** — `response_id`, `request_id`, `thread_id`, `session_id` are all `Identity` fields in the registry; `ValidateLabels` structurally refuses to let an `Identity` field be promoted to a stream label, so there is no config that removes them |
| Single query by response id returns metadata + content | **already satisfied** — same mechanism |
| Single query by thread id returns the conversation in order | **already satisfied** — `thread_id` on every line under both `codexlb.thread_id` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`, and each record type carries a deliberately chosen timestamp so time ordering reconstructs the conversation |
| Routing fields that explain the parameters | **partially** — `thread_source`, `subagent_kind`, `parent_thread_id` all reach metadata; `forked_from_thread_id` has no registry entry at all |
| `previous_response_id` emitted | **gap** — captured correctly by the reducer and present in the turn line's JSON body, but not structured metadata, so it is invisible to a LogQL metadata filter and absent from content lines entirely |
| Verified against the worked example | **done** — see below |

### The worked example still resolves, field for field

`resp_052b6a1e90eb18d3016a75b032be90819198bd170a3e118909` is still in the corpus and reproduces this issue's example exactly: model `gpt-5.6-sol`, effort `xhigh`, verbosity `low`, tier `default`, `thread_source=subagent`, `subagent_kind=thread_spawn`, `parent_thread_id=019fdb97-294e-…`, 208010 in / 490 out / 153 reasoning, cache ratio 0.978, thread `019fdb99-a66a-…`. No substitute turn was needed.

`TestCorpus_WorkedExample_Issue15` now pins it: it finds that turn in the whole-corpus reduction, asserts its identity before trusting anything derived from it, then asserts all four ids appear in structured metadata on **every** record type the turn actually produced — confirming `tool_call` and `tool_output` lines were genuinely exercised, not just the turn line. The assertions go through `kvMap`, the same dot-to-underscore translation the real push path applies, so it checks the wire representation a LogQL query would actually see rather than an intermediate form.

### The remaining gap, and the naming call it turned on

Two `Turn` fields are captured correctly but have no entry in the attribute registry, so `Guard.Metadata` never emits them: `PrevResponseID` and `ForkedFromThreadID`.

The key name for the first one is **not** a `codexlb.*` invention. `open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai` defines `gen_ai.request.previous_response.id`, and its note names OpenAI's `previous_response_id` explicitly as the example:

> The unique identifier of a previous response or interaction used to provide context for the current operation. … For example, `previous_response_id` in [OpenAI Responses API]

So it is `gen_ai.request.previous_response.id`. `forked_from_thread_id` has no GenAI equivalent and keeps `codexlb.forked_from_thread_id`. Both are `Identity` class — unbounded, structured metadata and span attributes only, never a metric attribute or a stream label.

Checking rather than recalling matters here specifically: three of five attribute names proposed on #18 turned out not to exist, and a `codexlb.*` name where the spec defines a standard one is exactly the divergence `TestNoUnjustifiedCodexlbKey` exists to catch.

Landing those two registry entries is the last item; it is held only because `internal/attr/names.go` is being edited concurrently for #23.

## Why

The telemetry is only worth emitting if something reads it. `codex-lb-overview` already exists and
covers the proxy's own view - this must **complement** it, not replace it (explicitly out of scope in
#1).

## Scope

Provisioned via `gcx` / `grafana-iac`, versioned here rather than clicked together.

**Dashboards** covering what only the wire capture knows:
- per-account rate-limit headroom and credits - the load-balancer view, never averaged across accounts
- token and cost shape by model, effort and thread source (user vs subagent)
- turn latency end to end, decomposed by critical path: pre-inference, engine wall, sampling/stream,
  client tool pause
- the agent tree: spawn rate, subagent depth, agent-message topology
- tool usage by name
- errors: `server_is_overloaded`, `websocket_connection_limit_reached` (the 60-minute connection cap),
  `previous_response_not_found`
- pipeline health: ingest lag, decode errors, sink rejections, drift findings

**Alerts:**
- ingest lag above threshold (the one that catches everything else)
- rate-limit headroom exhausted on any account
- `breaking` drift finding
- Loki rejections non-zero
- error-event rate

## Notes

- Dashboards must be able to exclude `baseline_reset` responses - their deltas are upper bounds that
  absorb unobserved work, not measurements.
- Same for `critical_path.coverage = missing_harness_boundary` (4.6%): those timings should be
  excluded or visibly marked rather than silently averaged in.
- Probe-family traffic (codex-lb's own health checks) must be excludable. It deliberately exercises
  the real models, so it cannot be separated by model - only by `family`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Dashboards provisioned as code, no manual panels.
- [ ] No panel duplicates `codex-lb-overview`.
- [ ] `baseline_reset` and `missing_harness_boundary` excludable, and excluded by default where they
      would distort an average.
- [ ] Probe family excluded from all user-facing panels.
- [ ] Alerts routed and tested.

Carried over from #17 (closed by 7f57ff8): **alert on `websocket_connection_limit_reached`.**

New as of 2026-08-07 and now a live value on `codexlb.errors{codexlb.error_code}`:

```
Responses websocket connection limit reached (60 minutes).
Create a new websocket connection to continue.
```

It is an OpenAI-side ceiling the traffic has started hitting, it gets more frequent as usage grows, and it has a documented remedy (recycle the connection before 60 minutes) — so it is exactly the shape of thing an alert catches early and a dashboard panel never gets looked at for.

Also worth a panel from the same issue: `codexlb.transport_events{frame_type, close_code}`. `frame_type=error` with no `close_code` is a connection dropped without a handshake (18 of 20 in the corpus); `close_code=1012` is OpenAI restarting a backend under us, which is not a codex-lb fault and should not page anyone.

title: Dashboards and alerts as code

body:
## Why

`clbprobe` (e3cb67d) can detect an archive format change in ~6 seconds across 1.4GB. Run by hand it
catches drift whenever someone remembers to run it. The failure it guards against is silent: a field
that gains a second JSON type makes Go's decoder abandon the whole event, which looks like slightly
fewer turns, not like an error.

## Scope

**In CI** - `clbprobe -full -fail-on breaking` against `corpus.sig.json`, so a corpus refresh that
changes the protocol fails the build. Skipped where no corpus is present.

**Against the live archive** - a scheduled run over codex-lb's actual archive directory, since that
is where a change appears first. Sampled mode is the right default at ~6s for a day of capture.

**As telemetry** - findings emitted as a metric,
`codexlb_archive_drift_findings{severity="breaking|new|info"}`, so drift becomes an alert rather than
a report nobody reads. A `breaking` finding should page; `new` should notify.

## Notes

- Sampling detects drift in common shapes and **proves nothing about rare ones** - the rarest real
  shapes occur ~10 times in 1.32M records. The scheduled job should sample; a `-full` pass belongs on
  a slower cadence or on demand once something is flagged.
- Absence findings are informational by design and must never page: a sampled scan not seeing
  something is the normal case.
- Baseline updates are a deliberate act. `-update` from a sampled scan is warned against for good
  reason; regenerating from `-full` is the only correct way to accept a change.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] CI job fails on a breaking finding where a corpus is available.
- [ ] Scheduled run against the live archive directory.
- [ ] Drift findings exposed as a metric by severity, with an alert on `breaking`.
- [ ] A protocol change deliberately injected into a fixture is caught end to end.

Follows on from e3cb67d.

comments.body:
CI landed in 69f4fb3; the drift-findings metric is the one item still open here.

**Done:**
- [x] CI job fails on a breaking finding where a corpus is available. This repo had **no `.github/` at all**, so `ci.yml` is the whole gate — gofmt, vet, build, test, then the probe.
- [x] Scheduled run against the live archive — committed, but **not live**: it needs a self-hosted runner on the tailnet that does not exist. The runner labels and the archive path are explicit placeholders in a header block rather than quietly wrong. Sampled-only, and it never passes `-update`, because accepting a sampled scan as a baseline would bake "rare shape absent" into `corpus.sig.json` as though it were confirmed gone.

**Still open:**
- [ ] Drift findings as a metric by severity, with an alert on `breaking`. It needs `internal/sink/otlpmetric`, which was being changed concurrently for #23 and is now being changed again for #8. The alert half is being built in #14 against the expected metric name.

**Two corrections to this issue's text, both found by running the tool rather than reading about it:**

**There is no `-full` flag.** This issue specifies `clbprobe -full -fail-on breaking`. A full scan is simply the default whenever `-sampled` is omitted. Checked against the binary's own `-h` output.

**`go run` destroys the exit-code contract this whole design depends on.** `clbprobe` documents `0` clean, `1` drift, `2` error, `3` nothing to do, and the workflow branches on all four. But `go run` does not propagate a child's exit code — it collapses every non-zero status to 1. Measured: the built binary returns 3 for an archive-less directory, `go run` returns 1 for the same input. Since 1 is the "breaking drift, fail the build" branch, running the probe through `go run` would have turned the normal no-corpus-in-CI case into a red build on **every single run**, with the exit-code handling reading as correct while doing nothing. The workflow builds the binary first.

One more subtlety worth recording: CI passes `corpus`, not `corpus/processed`. `corpus/sync` is tracked (`.gitignore` has an explicit `!/corpus/sync` exception) so the parent directory exists after checkout and yields exit 3 = nothing to scan; `corpus/processed` does not exist in CI at all and would yield exit 2 = error.
