body:
## Why

Extraction is otherwise complete - `clbprobe -full` over 1.56M lines reports 18 event types and none
unhandled. But a set of second-order timing fields inside `responsesapi.websocket_timing` is present
in the baseline (`corpus.sig.json`) and read by nothing.

## What is being dropped

**`taas_*` - the upstream-provider timing domain.** Four fields:
`timing_metrics.taas_request_to_provider_start_total_ms`,
`timing_metrics.taas_provider_start_to_first_token_total_ms`, and inside `critical_path`,
`taas_provider_wait_total_ms` and `taas_request_setup_total_ms`.

For a **load balancer** this is arguably the most interesting latency split in the whole capture: it
separates time spent waiting on the upstream provider from time the model spent generating. Slow
turns currently cannot be attributed to one or the other.

**`engine_service_*` vs `engine_iapi_*` - two parallel timing domains.** Only fragments of either are
read today: `engine_service_inference_total_ms`, `engine_service_sampling_total_ms`,
`engine_service_tbt_across_engine_calls_ms`, `engine_service_minus_iapi_tbt_across_engine_calls_ms`,
`engine_iapi_inference_total_ms`, `engine_iapi_sampling_total_ms`,
`engine_iapi_tbt_across_engine_calls_ms`.

**Per-tool-call durations.** `responsesapi_duration_excl_engine_per_tool_call_ms[]` is an array with a
`_truncated` companion flag - directly usable as tool spans in the traces phase.

**Others:** `inference_residual_total_ms`, `responses_duration_excl_engine_and_client_tool_time_ms`
and two sibling `responses_duration_excl_*` variants, `responsesapi_duration_excl_client_tools_ms`,
`responsesapi_chat_runner_streaming_token_batch_size`, `xapi_validation_time_s`,
`engine_total_prompt_tokens_total`, `engine_uncached_prompt_tokens_total`,
`timing_metrics.response_id`.

## The trap that applies to all of them

The outer `timing_metrics` block is `timing_scope: "logical_turn"` and **cumulative**, resetting at
the next turn - summing it raw overcounts ~5.7x. Any field added from the outer block needs the same
delta treatment the existing cumulative fields get. Fields under `critical_path` declare
`scope: "response"` and are already per-response; prefer those where both exist.

Note `taas_provider_start_to_first_token_total_ms` and `taas_request_to_provider_start_total_ms` were
absent from the 2026-08-07 hours while present on 2026-08-06 - they are not emitted on every response,
so they must be optional rather than assumed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `taas_*` captured, with outer-block fields delta-converted and `critical_path` fields taken
      per-response.
- [ ] Both engine timing domains captured completely rather than in fragments.
- [ ] Per-tool-call duration array captured with its truncation flag.
- [ ] Absent fields decode as absent, not as zero - a missing `taas_*` must not read as "0ms of
      provider wait".
- [ ] `clbprobe -full` still reports zero unhandled event types afterwards.

comments.body:
## Add `client_metadata.parent_turn_id`

Surfaced by `clbprobe` on the 2026-08-07 captures: `response.create` carries
`client_metadata.parent_turn_id`, which `frame.TurnMeta` does not decode.

It gives **turn-level** parenting where we currently only have thread-level
(`parent_thread_id`). That is a finer edge for the span model in #11 - it says which specific turn
spawned this one, not merely which thread.

Also new in the same captures, for the record: `originator` = `codex_exec`, and a `functions` tool
namespace wrapping `exec` / `request_user_input` / `wait`.

## Premise validated against the corpus before implementing, and it is partly wrong

Measured over all 16 archives (8,883 `responsesapi.websocket_timing` events, 103 threads, 220 series), classifying every field by whether it decreases within a `(thread_id, request_kind)` series — the same series key `turn.seriesKey` uses since #20. Three of the claims below I re-verified independently by hand against the raw corpus rather than trusting the analysis.

### The headline item cannot be delivered: every `taas_*` field is absent or null

This issue calls the `taas_*` split "arguably the most interesting latency split in the whole capture". It is not available:

| field | reality in the corpus |
|---|---|
| `taas_request_to_provider_start_total_ms` | **does not appear at all**, in any archive, including the 2026-08-06 ones this issue says carried it |
| `taas_provider_start_to_first_token_total_ms` | **does not appear at all**, same |
| `critical_path.taas_provider_wait_total_ms` | present as a key on 8,552 `critical_path` blocks, **value is `null` in every single one** |
| `critical_path.taas_request_setup_total_ms` | present as a key 8,552 times, **`null` every time** |

Verified by hand: `taas_provider_wait_total_ms\":null` is the *only* distinct form the field takes corpus-wide. Note the fields are escaped inside `payload.text`, so a naive `"taas_..."` search finds nothing and can look like absence for the wrong reason — that trap is worth knowing before anyone re-checks this.

`inference_residual_total_ms` is the same story: 8,552 occurrences, `null` every one. `xapi_validation_time_s` does not appear at all.

**So the "separate upstream-provider wait from model generation time" goal is not achievable from this capture.** Either the server stopped populating these, or they only populate for a deployment shape this traffic never hits. Not a coding task — the data is not there. Keeping the fields listed here as a watch item is the right disposition; `clbprobe` will now report it if they ever start carrying values.

### One field is already implemented

`engine_total_prompt_tokens_total` is listed here as dropped. It is not: `reducer.go:772` decodes it as `timingEvent.M.PromptTokensTotal` and diffs it into `EnginePromptTokensDelta`. Its `_uncached_` sibling genuinely is unread.

### One field carries no information

`responsesapi_chat_runner_streaming_token_batch_size` is present on all 8,883 events and is **exactly 0 every time** — one distinct value corpus-wide. Nothing to adopt.

### What is left, and how each must be handled

**Cumulative — needs delta treatment against the series baseline** (decrease-fraction 3.5–4.0%, matching the `num_engine_calls` control exactly, i.e. they only ever drop at a turn boundary):

`engine_service_inference_total_ms`, `engine_service_sampling_total_ms`, `engine_iapi_inference_total_ms`, `engine_iapi_sampling_total_ms`, `responses_duration_excl_engine_and_client_tool_time_ms`, `responses_duration_excl_engine_wait_and_sampling_ms`, `responses_duration_excl_engine_wait_and_sampling_iapi_ms`, `responsesapi_duration_excl_client_tools_ms`, `engine_uncached_prompt_tokens_total`.

The middle two are siblings this issue predicted but did not name; they exist and behave identically.

**Per-response — use directly, never delta:**

`engine_service_tbt_across_engine_calls_ms`, `engine_iapi_tbt_across_engine_calls_ms` (decrease-fraction 58–59%), and `engine_service_minus_iapi_tbt_across_engine_calls_ms` (44.7%, and it **goes negative**, min −6.70 — a monotonic sum cannot, which rules out cumulative on its own). These are running averages across engine calls rather than sums, so delta-ing them would be mathematically wrong regardless of what the scope declaration says.

**The array is cumulative and cannot be handled with scalar arithmetic.**

`responsesapi_duration_excl_engine_per_tool_call_ms` accumulates one entry per tool call across the whole logical turn, resetting only at the turn boundary. Proof: across 8,663 consecutive same-series pairs it shrank in exactly 300 — the *identical* numerator and denominator as `num_engine_calls`'s own decrease count, so it shrinks in precisely the responses where the reducer's existing turn-boundary detector fires. Correct handling is a suffix diff (the entries added since the previous response), not subtracting lengths or values. Lengths run 1–100; 36.8% of events carry more than 20.

Its companion flag is `responsesapi_duration_excl_engine_per_tool_call_truncated` — note it drops the `_ms` before `_truncated`, which is a naming trap. Present on all 8,883 events, `null` on 8,853, `true` on 30, never `false`.

### Method caveat worth carrying forward

Decrease-fraction cannot classify a TTFT-shaped field. `engine_service_ttft_total_ms` and `engine_iapi_ttft_total_ms` — both used directly in code today, correctly — score 3.75%, indistinguishable from the cumulative band, because they measure elapsed time *since turn start* and so trend upward across a turn without being sums. None of the fields classified above is TTFT-shaped, so the verdicts stand, but do not apply this method to a new elapsed-since-start field and believe the answer.

### Revised acceptance criteria

- [ ] The nine cumulative fields captured with delta treatment
- [ ] The three TBT fields captured per-response, undiffed
- [ ] Per-tool-call duration array captured by suffix diff, with its (correctly named) truncation flag
- [ ] Absent fields decode as absent, not zero — the existing `*float64` idiom in `timingEvent` already gives this
- [ ] `engine_uncached_prompt_tokens_total` added; `engine_total_prompt_tokens_total` already present, no change
- [ ] `clbprobe` still reports zero unhandled event types
- [ ] ~~`taas_*` captured~~ — **not deliverable, see above**; recorded as a watch item instead

Closed by 4968921. What landed, against the revised criteria in the comment above:

- [x] Nine cumulative fields delta-treated through the existing `applyTiming` mechanism and series baseline — not a second mechanism
- [x] Three TBT fields per-response, undiffed
- [x] Per-tool-call duration array suffix-diffed, with the correctly-named `..._per_tool_call_truncated` flag
- [x] Absent decodes as absent — the `*float64`/`*int` idiom in `timingEvent` throughout
- [x] `engine_uncached_prompt_tokens_total` added; `engine_total_prompt_tokens_total` was already implemented, no change
- [x] `clbprobe` still reports zero unhandled event types (19 seen, 0 unnamed)
- [x] `taas_*` recorded as a watch item rather than implemented — not deliverable, the data is null or absent

**One thing this issue did not cover and which is now #23:** the capture stops at the reducer. The fields reach Loki for free, because `turnLine` marshals every scalar on `Turn`, but they reach no metric and no span. For a load balancer the latency split is the point of having it, so leaving it Loki-only is not finished — it is the same "the data arrives but has nowhere to go" state #17 was in before it was closed.

**`stateVersion` moved 2 → 3**, which this issue did not ask for and which is load-bearing. It is not a key change and a v2 snapshot decodes without error — that is precisely why the version had to move. Every new baseline would restore as zero against a server counter sitting at its real accumulated value, so the first response after a restart would report a whole turn's inference time as its own delta. Worse, the series would read as already-seen, so `BaselineReset` would not fire and the over-count would carry no flag marking it an upper bound. Same silent shape as #20, arriving through the checkpoint instead of the series key. Discarding the snapshot costs one flagged cold-start turn per series.

title: Adopt the timing_metrics domains still being dropped

body:
## Why

#1 parked traces as out of scope. The full-corpus profiling done since has changed the picture: the
capture contains a **complete trace model**, and this is the one signal nothing else in the stack can
produce. codex-lb's 60 Prometheus families are proxy internals; `request_logs` is per-request
metadata. Neither can answer "this turn took 90 seconds - where did it go, and which subagent caused
it".

Sequenced **after** #5 and #7, per decision 2026-08-07. The attribute-contract work (#3) should be
designed with spans in mind so this is not a retrofit.

## The model the data supports

| span | source |
|---|---|
| thread | `thread_id`, with `parent_thread_id` / `forked_from_thread_id` giving the agent tree |
| logical turn | server `turn_id` from `client_metadata` (authoritative), `turn_started_at_unix_ms` as the true start |
| response | `response_id`, `ServerCreatedAt` -> `ServerCompletedAt`, chained by `previous_response_id` into a DAG |
| critical-path phases | `responses_pre_inference_ms`, `engine_wall_ms`, `sampling_and_stream_total_ms`, `client_tool_pause_ms`, `responses_other_ms` - already per-response, `scope: "response"` |
| tool calls | `responsesapi_duration_excl_engine_per_tool_call_ms[]` is a per-tool-call duration array, already span-shaped |

Span **links** between agent threads come from `agent_message` author -> recipient (191 distinct pairs
observed), which is the real multi-agent topology and exists nowhere else in the capture.

## Traps carried over

- The turn id must come from `response.create`'s `client_metadata`, **not** the
  `x-codex-turn-metadata` header. The header is stamped at websocket connect and never updated;
  trusting it labels 89% of real turns as `prewarm` with an empty turn id.
- `traceparent` is the **client's per-connection** trace, constant across every frame of a connection.
  It is connection context, not a per-turn trace id. Do not root spans on it without deciding what it
  actually means.
- `critical_path.coverage` is `missing_harness_boundary` on 4.6% of responses. Those durations are not
  trustworthy and the span should say so rather than draw a confident bar.
- Spans are emitted from an archive that is minutes to hours old. Tempo accepts historical spans, but
  confirm the ingestion window before assuming a backlog replays cleanly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Trace/span ids derived deterministically from archive ids, so re-processing is idempotent
      rather than duplicating traces.
- [ ] Subagent threads appear as children of the spawning thread; verified against a corpus thread
      with a known `spawn_agent`.
- [ ] Critical-path phase durations sum to the parent span within a stated tolerance, or the span is
      marked incomplete.
- [ ] `missing_harness_boundary` responses visibly flagged.
- [ ] Trace volume and Tempo cost measured on a corpus replay before enabling continuously.
title: P7 - traces to Tempo: the agent tree and where a turn's time went

body:
## Why

The service currently runs only from a foreground binary. It needs to ship as a container that comes up alongside codex-lb.

## Decision (2026-08-07, binding)

**Docker image + compose fragment, added to codex-lb's own services section**, so codexlb2otel starts and stops with codex-lb on camden. NOT a systemd unit - explicitly ruled out.

**Do not deploy until the backlog is substantially implemented.** The service has been verified working end to end by hand (see #1's emit-wave comment); shipping it is deliberately the last step, not the next one.

## Scope

- Multi-stage Dockerfile, static build, non-root user, no shell in the final layer.
- Image published to GHCR on release, tagged by version and by digest.
- A compose fragment for codex-lb's stack: the archive directory mounted **read-only** (the service must never be able to damage the only copy of the raw capture), a writable volume for the checkpoint only.
- Credentials by env from codex-lb's existing `.env` pattern, never baked into the image and never in the compose file. The lab already resolves both tokens from a single `GRAFANA_TOKEN`.
- Config file mounted read-only; `config.example.yaml` is the documented starting point.
- Healthcheck wired to the existing loopback endpoint.
- release-please for versioning, with the `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN` PAT so bot-authored release PRs run CI unattended.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `docker compose up` inside codex-lb's stack brings the service up healthy against the real archive path.
- [ ] Archive mount is read-only, asserted in the compose fragment.
- [ ] No credential appears in the image, in `docker inspect`, or in the compose file.
- [ ] Container stops cleanly on SIGTERM within the compose stop grace period, flushing before the checkpoint (the invariant #4 already pins at the service level).
- [ ] Image runs as non-root.
- [ ] Restart resumes from the checkpoint without re-shipping or skipping - verified against a real archive, not asserted.

comments.body:
Closed by cfc27d5. **Nothing is deployed** — the artifacts exist and are verified locally; shipping remains the deliberate last step.

### The healthcheck is the part worth reading

The image is `distroless/static:nonroot`, which has no shell and no HTTP client. The obvious way to give it a `HEALTHCHECK` is to copy busybox's `wget` applet in — and that quietly defeats the reason for using distroless at all.

busybox is **one multi-call ELF that dispatches on `argv[0]`**, hardlinked under every applet name it implements. Copy it in as `wget` and anything with code execution inside the container can `execve("/usr/local/bin/wget", ["sh", "-c", ...])` and get a shell. It passes the test everyone runs — `docker run --entrypoint sh` fails, nothing is *named* `sh` — while leaving a working shell in the image. Renaming a shell is not removing one.

So the probe is a `-healthcheck` flag on the service binary that is already in the image. That costs nothing and fixes a second problem: it loads the same config the server does, so it probes whatever `health.listen` is actually deployed. A host:port baked into the Dockerfile would silently probe the wrong address the moment a deployment overrode it, report unhealthy, and **restart-loop the container over a config mismatch**.

`health.Probe` fails closed on every non-200 path — not-ready (the 503 served while starting and while draining), unreachable, empty listen address. Failing open on any of those would report a service that has stopped polling as fine, which is exactly what #8's ingest-lag metric exists to catch.

### Acceptance

- [x] Archive mount read-only, asserted in the fragment — `read_only: true` confirmed via `docker compose config`
- [x] No credential in the image, in `docker inspect`, or in the compose file — variable references only
- [x] Container stops cleanly on SIGTERM, flushing before the checkpoint — **exit 0**, with `stopped polling; draining sink` in the logs
- [ ] `docker compose up` inside codex-lb's stack against the real archive path — **not done, this is deployment**

### Measured

| check | result |
|---|---|
| image size | **6.1 MB** |
| `docker run --entrypoint sh` | fails: `exec: "sh": executable file not found in $PATH` |
| configured user | `65532:65532`, confirmed running as that uid, not just declared |
| Docker health status | `healthy` |
| SIGTERM | exit 0, drain logged |

The first attempt at that verification failed for a good reason worth recording: the service **correctly refuses to start when every sink is disabled** (`every sink is disabled; the service would tail the archive and discard it`). The container was unhealthy because the service was right, not because the healthcheck was wrong.

### release-please

The release PR is opened under `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN`, not the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` — a bot-authored PR does not auto-run workflows that pull code from another repository; they park behind a manual approval gate and the PR sits with stuck checks forever. This repo's CI is first-party-only today so the trap does not bite yet; it is wired now rather than left as a landmine. The secret is provisioned. All third-party actions are pinned by commit SHA with the tag verified against the API, not copied blind.

### Three inputs still need a human before deployment

1. **The archive path on camden.** `config.example.yaml` reads as a host bind-mount path, but codex-lb's own compose mounts its data through a **named volume**. Those are not obviously the same thing — needs `docker inspect` against the real container.
2. **The token env var name** — the fragment assumes `GRAFANA_TOKEN` per this issue's own text; confirm against the real `.env.local`.
3. **The config file path** on camden.

Also: the fragment's image tag reads `0.0.0` until release-please cuts a first real version, so it is not pullable yet regardless.

**Operational note:** do not run `docker compose config` or `up` for this service in a shell with real secrets exported unless you are deliberate about where stdout goes — compose substitutes live shell variables into its rendered output.

## Two of the three unresolved inputs are now answered against camden (eb373a1)

**1. The archive is a bind mount** — confirmed by Rob and verified. `docker inspect` on the running codex-lb container reports exactly one mount:

```
Type "bind", Source /opt/codex-lb/data/codex-lb,
Destination /var/lib/codex-lb, Mode "rw,Z"
```

So the archive is `/opt/codex-lb/data/codex-lb/conversation-archive` on the **host** (19 files present, current through `2026-08-07T18`) and `/var/lib/codex-lb/conversation-archive` inside codex-lb's own container. That host path is also `config.example.yaml`'s `archive.dir` default, so the fragment binds host path to an identical container path and the shipped config needs no override. The named-volume alternative is deleted rather than left as a live option.

**A trap that inspect surfaced, now warned about in the fragment:** codex-lb's mount carries `Mode "rw,Z"`. `Z` relabels content with an SELinux label **private to the mounting container**. Copying that flag onto this service's mount would relabel codex-lb's own data directory out from under it and break the service this one exists to observe — the same "must never be able to damage the only copy of the raw capture" failure the read-only mount guards against, arriving through a flag rather than through a write. It is moot today because **SELinux is Disabled on camden** (Fedora 44 Server), which is also why codex-lb's own `Z` is inert. If SELinux is ever enabled, this mount wants lowercase `z` or no flag at all — never `Z`.

**2. There is no `GRAFANA_TOKEN`, and this issue's text is wrong about it.**

This issue states "The lab already resolves both tokens from a single `GRAFANA_TOKEN`". No such variable exists on camden. The real convention is a **per-service `.env` with prefixed names**:

| service | file | token variable |
|---|---|---|
| opnsense2otel | `/opt/opnsense2otel/.env` | `OPN2OTEL_OTLP_GRAFANA_CLOUD_TOKEN` |
| tailscale2otel | `/opt/tailscale2otel/.env` | `TS2OTEL_OTLP__GRAFANA_CLOUD__TOKEN` |

and codex-lb's own `.env` carries neither. Following that pattern gives codexlb2otel `/opt/codexlb2otel/.env` with `CODEXLB2OTEL_`-prefixed names — which is exactly what `config.example.yaml`'s `${...}` indirections already expect, so nothing else has to change and no second credential gets invented.

The fragment now uses `env_file:` rather than `environment:` with `${...}`. Compose expands `${...}` from the **shell that invokes it**, so a variable that shell cannot see silently becomes an empty string and the service starts with an unset token, failing later at push time rather than at startup. `env_file` is read from disk regardless of who runs compose. It is left **required**, so a missing credentials file fails loudly — which does mean `docker compose config` fails anywhere the file is absent, including a laptop. That is the correct behaviour, not a defect.

## Still outstanding before deployment

1. **The config file path on camden** — the fragment assumes `./codexlb2otel/config.yaml` relative to codex-lb's compose file. Copy `config.example.yaml` there and edit it; never edit `config.example.yaml` in place.
2. **`/opt/codexlb2otel/.env` has to be created** on camden with `CODEXLB2OTEL_LOKI_TOKEN` and `CODEXLB2OTEL_OTLP_TOKEN`. CI deploys code and config only, never secrets.
3. **A real release.** The image tag reads `0.0.0` until release-please cuts one — PR #25, now proposing **0.1.0** rather than 1.0.0, awaiting a human merge.

## Publishing moved to the shared fleet pipeline (fc7d893, d331267)

The hand-rolled `docker.yml` is gone. `publish.yml` is now a thin wrapper around `rknightion/.github`'s `container-publish.yml`, so this repo behaves like every other `*2otel` service rather than being the one doing its own thing.

What that buys, none of which the hand-rolled version had: **native per-arch amd64 + arm64 runners** with a manifest-list merge (not QEMU, which mis-resolves native libs), cosign keyless signing, SBOMs attached to the release, and a Trivy scan into the Security tab.

Verified on the published image:

```
mediaType: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json
  linux/arm64  sha256:c0e5d583e17ca053fc9
  linux/amd64  sha256:c2588319b179ea91a9a
```

### Two publishing modes, and camden tracks the first

- **Edge** — every push to `main`, producing `:main` and `:main-<sha>`. **This is what camden pins**, with watchtower pulling updates, so a merge to `main` is what reaches the host, not a release.
- **Release** — called by `release-please` once it cuts one, producing `:X.Y.Z`, `:X.Y`, `:X`, `:latest`.

The compose fragment therefore pins **`:main`**, and release-please no longer rewrites that line — the `x-release-please-version` marker and the `extra-files` entry are removed. A version pinned there would defeat watchtower and freeze the host at whatever the last release happened to be. Docs and `dashboards/` changes are excluded from the edge trigger so a README tweak does not roll a new image out to camden for nothing.

### The cross-repo bot-PR trap now genuinely applies here

`uses: rknightion/.github/...` is exactly the shape GitHub refuses to auto-run on a bot-authored PR — it parks at `action_required` behind "Approve and run" indefinitely. It was harmless while this repo's CI was first-party-only; it is not any more. `release-please.yml` already opens its PR under `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN`, a trusted PAT identity, and that secret is provisioned. **That step must not be simplified back to `GITHUB_TOKEN`.**

### Three bugs the switch removed or exposed

1. **The old publish job could not check out its own repo.** A job-level `permissions:` block *replaces* the workflow-level one, so listing only `packages: write` set `contents` to `none`; on a private repo `actions/checkout` then failed with `Repository not found`, which reads like a typo in the repo name.
2. **The old workflow published an image with no version tag.** `type=semver` derives from the git ref, and this pipeline never runs on a tag push — release-please calls it *after* the release exists, so the ref is `refs/heads/main`. It matched nothing and emitted no version tag **without failing**, so `v0.1.0` went green while producing an image the compose fragment could not pull.
3. **The same permissions trap immediately recurred** in the new `publish.yml`, because `permissions: {}` at the top denies everything and the extra `go-version` job had no block of its own. Fixed, with the reason written on the job.

`GO_VERSION` is read from `go.mod` and passed as a build arg rather than relying on the Dockerfile's fallback — same rule `ci.yml` follows via `setup-go`'s `go-version-file`.

### Remaining

Publish runs are **red at the final attestation step** — see #27, where the decision to leave it for now is recorded. The image publishes fine regardless.

The GHCR package is public, so camden needs no pull credential. The only thing still outstanding before deployment is the config file path on camden.

## All three unresolved inputs are now closed (bc2db02)

| input | resolution |
|---|---|
| archive path / mount type | **bind mount**, `/opt/codex-lb/data/codex-lb/conversation-archive`, verified via `docker inspect` |
| credentials | `/opt/codexlb2otel/.env`, created — `root:root`, `0600`, `CODEXLB2OTEL_{LOKI,OTLP,AGENTO11Y}_TOKEN`, following the per-service convention the sibling exporters use |
| config file path | `/opt/codex-lb/codexlb2otel.config.yaml`, created — beside codex-lb's own `compose.yml` |

The config is a **straight copy of `config.example.yaml` with no edits**, which is worth recording because it means the example is genuinely correct for this host rather than merely illustrative: `archive.dir` and `archive.checkpoint` already match the mounts, `health.listen` stays on loopback where the in-container healthcheck reaches it and nothing else does, and both tokens are `${...}` references that the `.env` satisfies.

It is named `codexlb2otel.config.yaml`, not `config.yaml`, because that directory already holds codex-lb's own `compose.yml`, `.env` and `README.md` — a bare `config.yaml` among them would read as codex-lb's own.

`agento11y` is **not** enabled: `config.example.yaml` has no section for it, so it defaults off. The `.env` already carries a token for it, so enabling it later is a config edit and a restart, nothing more.

## What deployment now consists of

Everything is in place on camden. The remaining steps are all Rob's:

1. Merge the `codexlb2otel:` service and the `codexlb2otel-checkpoint` volume from this repo's `docker-compose.yml` into `/opt/codex-lb/compose.yml` — or run it alongside with a second `-f`.
2. `docker compose up -d codexlb2otel`.
3. Confirm `docker compose ps` reports healthy, and that data arrives in Grafana. **A 2xx is not delivery in any of the three protocols here** — Loki returns 204 for a line it discarded, sigil reports OTLP `partial_success`, and agento11y returns per-item `accepted` flags — so read it back with `gcx --context m7kni` rather than trusting the push.

Nothing has been deployed. Two things worth watching on the first real run, both of which only appear against live data:

- **Ingest lag** (`codexlb.selfobs.ingest_lag_seconds`) is the metric that catches every other failure first, and it has never seen a real archive.
- **The first checkpoint write.** Restart-resume is tested, but never against camden's actual archive directory with files still being appended to.

## Fragment merged into camden's compose file, and it needed three fixes to be runnable

`c06983e`. The `codexlb2otel:` service block is now in `/opt/codex-lb/compose.yml` (backup at `compose.yml.bak-20260807-204433`), `docker compose config -q` passes, and the image is pulled. **Nothing is started** - `up -d` is still deliberately the last step.

Three things this issue's packaging had wrong, all found by checking the host rather than by reasoning:

**1. uid 65532 cannot read the archive.** codex-lb writes it as its own uid, so the directory is `drwx------ rob rob` and every file is `0600 rob rob`. No group bit, no other bit. Measured with a throwaway container against the real bind mount:

| uid | result |
| --- | --- |
| 1000 | lists 20 files, reads `1f8b` (gzip magic) off the newest |
| 65532 | `ls: can't open '/a': Permission denied` |

This is the dangerous shape: the service would have started cleanly, found an empty directory, and reported nothing forever. Now pinned `user: "1000:1000"`. Still non-root, still no shell. Loosening the archive's permissions instead was rejected - they are codex-lb's, on the only copy of the raw capture.

Host permissions on the *parent* path (`/opt/codex-lb` is root-only) are irrelevant: a bind mount attaches the source directory itself, so only its own mode is consulted inside the container.

**2. That breaks the checkpoint volume.** A fresh named volume takes ownership from the image's directory at the mount point, and the image deliberately creates none - Docker would make it `root:root 0755` and the first checkpoint write would `EACCES`. Swapped to a relative bind, `./data/codexlb2otel`, created `0750 rob:rob`. Also matches the convention codex-lb's own compose already uses.

**3. It breaks the config file too, and this one actually bit.** Installed `root:root 0640`, copied from the sibling files in that directory, and the container exited with `config: read /etc/codexlb2otel/config.yaml: permission denied`. `env_file` is unaffected because the **daemon** reads it as root before the container exists; a bind-mounted config file is read by the process itself. Now `root:1000 0640` - root owns it so only root can edit, group 1000 so the service can read it.

Verified after the fix: `-healthcheck` against the deployed config file gets all the way past `config.Load` (which runs `Validate`) and fails only on the probe's `connection refused`, which is the correct answer for a service that is not running.

**Watchtower needs no label.** It runs here with no `--label-enable`, so it watches everything by default and `:main` rolls out on its hourly pass. codex-lb carries `watchtower.enable=false` because it is built locally from `./src`; this service is the opposite case.

**Unrelated observation, not acted on:** codex-lb's own compose has a comment under `volumes:` saying the conversation archive lives on the Synology via the `soft` NFS mount, referencing `CODEX_LB_CONVERSATION_ARCHIVE_DIR` in `.env`. That variable is not set (only `CODEX_LB_CONVERSATION_ARCHIVE_ENABLED=true`), `/mnt/codex-lb-archive` is mounted but **empty**, and the live archive is the local `/opt/codex-lb/data/codex-lb/conversation-archive` (20 files, newest written 20:41 today). The comment describes an intent that was never wired. Left alone - it is codex-lb's file, not this project's - but worth knowing, because if that move ever happens this fragment's bind source moves with it.

### What starting it consists of

```
cd /opt/codex-lb && docker compose up -d codexlb2otel
```

Then read the data back with `gcx --context m7kni` rather than trusting the pushes: a 2xx is not delivery in any of the three protocols here. `codexlb.selfobs.ingest_lag_seconds` is the metric that catches every other failure first, and it has never seen a real archive.

## Why

Phase P5 of #1. Postgres `request_logs` knows things the wire capture cannot: `cost_usd`, the
resolved `api_key_id`, and codex-lb's own view of the request. This is an **enrichment** source only.

**Do not re-derive `request_logs`.** It already carries cost, latency, tokens, service tier and error
codes, and already drives the `codex-lb-overview` dashboard. Duplicating it is explicitly out of scope
in #1.

## Scope

- Join archive turns to `request_logs` and attach `cost_usd` and `api_key_id`.
- LRU-cached; the join key and its hit rate need measuring before this is trusted.
- **Degrades gracefully**: Postgres being unreachable must reduce the telemetry, never stop it. The
  archive pipeline is the primary source and must keep running with enrichment absent.

## Open question to resolve first

What actually joins them. The archive has `request_id` in two namespaces (`ws_<hex32>` and bare UUID -
both valid, do not "fix" this), plus `response_id` and the server `turn_id`. Confirm against a live
`request_logs` row which of these is present there, and measure the join hit rate on the corpus before
building anything.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Join key identified against live data, with the measured hit rate recorded on this issue.
- [ ] Postgres unavailable = enrichment absent, pipeline healthy; asserted by test.
- [ ] Cache hit rate exposed as a metric.
- [ ] No field re-derived that `request_logs` already publishes.

comments.body:
## Join key resolved against live data: `request_logs.archive_request_id`

Queried read-only on camden (`codex-lb-postgres-1`) 2026-08-07.

`request_logs` has an **`archive_request_id`** column holding exactly the archive's own
`request_id`. Confirmed on a single response and then at volume:

| | |
|---|---|
| rows in the last 48h | 22,819 |
| rows with `archive_request_id` | **22,819 (100.00%)** |
| prefix breakdown | `ws_` 22,620, UUID 199 |

**The join is 1:1 and complete.** No fuzzy matching, no timestamp windowing, no LRU heuristics
needed. `archive_request_id` is the key; nothing else is required.

Worked example - `resp_052b6a1e90eb18d3016a75b032be90819198bd170a3e118909`, cross-checked against
`clbfind` output from the archive:

| field | Postgres | archive | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `request_id` | `resp_052b6a...118909` | `response_id` | match |
| `archive_request_id` | `ws_481fa8fa32724155a2ff8f372d7448ce` | `request_id` | **the join key** |
| `conversation_id` | `019fdb99-a66a-7841-a420-e9f8602d4034` | `thread_id` | match |
| `session_id` | `019fdb97-294e-...` | `session_id` | match |
| model / effort | `gpt-5.6-sol` / `xhigh` | same | match |
| input / cached / output / reasoning tokens | 208010 / 203520 / 490 / 153 | identical | match |
| plan / service tier | `pro` / `default` | same | match |
| `latency_ms` | 13338 | elapsed 13.0s | match |
| **`cost_usd`** | **0.13891** | absent | the enrichment |
| **`api_key_id`** | **42faf97e-...** | absent | the enrichment |

Independent derivations from two entirely separate sources agreeing on every token count is strong
evidence the reducer is correct.

## Three traps found while confirming it

**1. `account_id` is NOT equal across the two sources.** Postgres appends an 8-hex suffix:

```
Postgres: bd537096-499f-46f4-b1d8-20b1994b9ac5_1369f6ad
archive:  bd537096-499f-46f4-b1d8-20b1994b9ac5
```

All three accounts follow the pattern (`..._1369f6ad`, `..._a58aa3d0`, `..._f6afa612`). An equality
join on `account_id` returns nothing, silently. Enrichment must join on `archive_request_id` only,
and any per-account grouping across the two sources has to normalise the suffix first.

**2. `request_kind` uses different vocabularies.** Postgres has exactly two values over 48h -
`normal` (17,292) and `prewarm` (5,527). The archive has three - `turn`, `prewarm`, `compaction`.
Postgres has **no notion of compaction at all**, so the archive sees a distinction the database
cannot express. Do not map one onto the other; keep both, named distinctly.

**3. TTFT means different things in each source and the numbers differ by 4.4x.** For the response
above: Postgres `latency_first_token_ms` = **5631**, archive TTFT = **1219**. `latency_ms` (13338)
and archive elapsed (13.0s) agree, so this is not a clock problem - the archive figure is
engine-side, the Postgres figure is proxy-observed and includes what happens before the engine
starts. Both are correct and they answer different questions. Emitting them under one name is how
"our two TTFT panels disagree" becomes an incident.

## Consequences

- The LRU cache in the original scope is unnecessary complexity for a 1:1 indexed lookup. Batch the
  join by `archive_request_id` instead.
- Only `cost_usd` and `api_key_id` are genuinely additive. Everything else `request_logs` holds is
  already in the archive and verified identical - so per #1, do not re-derive it.
- Confirm `archive_request_id` is indexed before joining at volume.

Updated acceptance criteria:

- [x] Join key identified against live data, with the measured hit rate recorded (100%, 22,819 rows)
- [ ] Enrichment attaches `cost_usd` and `api_key_id` only
- [ ] `account_id` suffix normalised, or per-account grouping kept to one source
- [ ] Postgres `request_kind` and archive `request_kind` kept as distinct fields
- [ ] The two TTFT measurements named distinctly, never merged
- [ ] Postgres unavailable = enrichment absent, pipeline healthy; asserted by test

## Blocking question answered: join key confirmed and hit rate measured

Full measurement, not a sample. The whole 16-archive corpus reduced with the real reducer (8,931 turns) joined against the **entire** `request_logs` table (53,454 rows, id columns only, no message content pulled). `request_logs` covers 2026-08-03 12:13 → 2026-08-07 17:48, which fully contains the corpus window, so nothing was excluded by retention. Read-only throughout: SELECT only, no writes, no schema changes.

### The join key

**`request_logs.archive_request_id` = archive `request_id`, exact string match, both namespaces, no transformation.** Unique across all 53,454 rows, so no fan-out.

The alternate — `request_logs.request_id` = archive `response_id` — **also works**, at the same rate wherever the archive has a `response_id` at all.

`conversation_id` = archive `thread_id` and `session_id` = `session_id` both confirmed at 100% where populated, so this issue's table on #3 is correct in every row.

### Hit rate, whole corpus, by request_kind × family

| request_kind | family | N | via `archive_request_id` | via `response_id` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| turn | websocket | 8,548 | 100% | 99.9% |
| turn | http | 197 | 100% | 98.5% |
| prewarm | websocket | 104 | 100% | 100% |
| compaction | websocket | 37 | 100% | 100% |
| memory | websocket | 16 | 100% | 100% |
| memory | http | 12 | 100% | 100% |
| compaction | http | 2 | 100% | 100% |
| none | unknown | 13 | n/a — no request_id at all | n/a |

**The shortfall in the `response_id` column is not a join failure.** Every miss is a turn that never had a `response_id` — status `transport`/`error`/`incomplete`, where the server died before returning one. Exclude those and it is also 100%. `archive_request_id` is populated on every turn that has any `request_id`, including the failed ones, so it correlates error turns that the other key cannot reach at all.

The 13 unmatched turns carry no `request_id` in their frames — corpus-boundary artifacts. They still join on `thread_id`/`session_id`.

### The two namespaces join identically

`ws_<hex32>`: 8,705/8,705. Bare UUID (only `family=http`): 213/213. Postgres stores both verbatim in `archive_request_id` (52,334 prefixed, 1,120 bare, no cross-contamination). Confirmed there is nothing to "fix" here, as #3 already suspected.

### `cost_usd` and `api_key_id`

- **`cost_usd`** — `double precision`, null on 266/53,454 (0.50%), and the nulls are **fully explained**: exclusively `status IN ('error','cancelled')`. Every `success` row has a cost. A null means "never billed", not "missing".
- **`api_key_id`** — `varchar`, null on 27/53,454 (0.05%), all `normal`+`error`. **Cardinality 2**, confirmed against the `api_keys` table itself, which has exactly 2 rows. So it is bounded by provisioning, like `account_id` — safe as a metric attribute. That resolves this issue's stated worry, but the safety rests on "bounded by how many keys the operator provisions", which belongs in the field's comment as an assumption rather than being silently relied on.

### ⚠️ `archive_request_id` has NO INDEX

Confirmed via `\d request_logs`. The existing indexes cover `request_id`, `conversation_id`, `account_id`, `api_key_id` — not `archive_request_id`. **A per-turn lookup on the natural join key would full-table-scan 53,454 rows on every cache miss, against codex-lb's live production database.** That turns an enrichment nicety into an operational problem on camden.

Two ways out, and this is the decision the design now hinges on:

1. **Add an index on `archive_request_id`.** A schema change on codex-lb's own database — out of scope for a read-only investigation, needs a deliberate decision.
2. **Join on `request_id = response_id` instead**, which *is* indexed and has the identical hit rate once error turns are excluded. Costs the ability to enrich `transport`/`error`/`incomplete` turns — which is a real loss, since those are exactly the ones worth understanding.

Recommendation: option 2 first, because it needs no change to somebody else's production schema and the pipeline must degrade gracefully anyway. Revisit the index if enriching failed turns turns out to matter.

### Naming trap for whoever writes the join

**`request_logs.request_kind` is NOT the archive's `request_kind`.** Postgres has only `normal` and `prewarm`, collapsing the archive's `turn`/`compaction`/`memory` into `normal`. Anyone will reach for the same-named column on both sides and expect them to line up. They do not. There is also a mostly-empty `connection_request_kind` (~27% populated) that looks like an in-flight migration — do not build against it without checking its backfill state.

### Worth enriching with, beyond the two named

All genuinely absent from the wire capture, because they are codex-lb's own routing decisions: `model_source_id`/`model_source_kind`; `upstream_proxy_pool_id`/`_endpoint_id`/`_route_mode`/`_fallback_used`/`_fail_closed_reason`; `client_ip`/`useragent`/`useragent_group`; `failure_phase`/`failure_exception_type`/`upstream_status_code`/`upstream_error_code`; the prewarm detail columns; and `requested_service_tier` vs `actual_service_tier` — the archive carries only the actual one, so the ask-versus-got distinction is new information.

**Leave alone** (already in `Turn`, often finer-grained): model, status, reasoning_effort, service_tier, plan_type, the latency family, token counts, error code and message.

### Not established

- Whether the join holds outside this 4-day window, or for a `family=probe` turn (none appeared in this corpus).
- Whether `archive_request_id` is ever written late or transiently absent — only a point-in-time snapshot was examined, no mid-flight request was caught.
- Retention/rollup behaviour over a longer horizon.
- Production performance of the intended cached-lookup pattern under load; correctness was validated offline, not throughput.

- [x] Join key identified against live data, with the measured hit rate recorded on this issue

## Why

`genai-otel-bridge` is self-observing and this should be too. One metric matters more than the rest:
**ingest lag** - the gap between the newest record processed and now. Every other failure mode of this
service is visible as lag first. A watcher that has silently stopped, a checkpoint that is not
advancing, a sink rejecting everything - all of them look like lag growing.

## Scope

Emit alongside the derived telemetry, on the same OTLP pipeline:

- **`ingest_lag_seconds`** - now minus the newest record timestamp seen. The alert.
- files watched, current file, checkpoint offset per file
- bytes read, gzip members decoded, lines decoded, undecodable lines
- partial-member reads (normal steady state, not an error) vs genuine decode errors
- file replacements detected (`Stats.FilesReplaced`), files reclaimed/deleted
- turns emitted, turns evicted without `response.completed`, open-response map size (a leak here is
  the failure mode `Flush`/`Evict` exist to prevent)
- sink batches, failures by reason, retries, dropped records
- reducer state size after snapshot

## Notes

- Eviction is measured against the **newest record seen**, never `time.Now()`. Catching up on a
  backlog would otherwise evict every in-flight response on the first pass purely because the archive
  is hours old, while the completions sit in the next chunk. Found by the incremental-append test,
  not by inspection - do not regress it.
- The archive writer silently drops records under disk pressure (`_archive_disk_pressure_active()`).
  Gaps are expected and are not corruption; do not alert on them as such.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ingest_lag_seconds` emitted, verified against a deliberately stale directory.
- [ ] Decode errors distinguished from partial-member reads in both metrics and logs.
- [ ] Open-response map size exposed, so a leak is visible before it is an outage.
- [ ] Sink failures counted by reason.
title: Self-observability, and ingest lag above all

## Why

Phase P4 of #1. Direct OTLP push to `https://otlp-gateway-prod-gb-south-1.grafana.net/otlp`
(instance `<GRAFANA_STACK_ID>`).

## Ground truth (settled, do not re-litigate)

**Temporality is cumulative.** Mimir 3.0 has native delta OTLP ingestion but its own docs mark it
experimental and it is not enableable on managed Grafana Cloud. The reducer already emits per-response
**deltas**, which are the natural argument to an OTel `Counter.Add()`; the SDK aggregates to cumulative
for export, and a restart resets the counter with a fresh start time, which is correct counter-reset
semantics. **Metrics therefore need no checkpoint** - the checkpoint exists only for within-turn delta
correctness and for not re-shipping logs.

## Candidate instruments

Counters (all summed from per-response values that are already safe to sum):
- tokens: input, output, reasoning, cached, cache_write, total
- responses by status; turns by request_kind (`prewarm` and `compaction` are **not** user turns and
  counting them as such overstates turn rates and understates cost per turn)
- engine calls (both the delta arithmetic and `critical_path.num_engine_calls`, which agreed 212/212
  on the fixture and can cross-check each other)
- tool calls by name; web-search requests; image-gen tokens
- errors by type/code; websocket close codes; transport events
- safety-buffering events (4 in 4000 - rare and exactly what you want to see)

Histograms:
- TTFT, `engine_wall_ms`, `harness_unblocked_ms`, `pre_inference_ms`, `sampling_and_stream_ms`,
  `client_tool_pause_ms`
- end-to-end turn latency, from the client's `turn_started_at_unix_ms` to `ServerCompletedAt` - the
  only figure that measures what the user actually waited for
- streaming shape: text-delta count, time-between-tokens

Gauges - **the headline for a load balancer**, and meaningless unless grouped by `account_id`:
- rate-limit used percent, primary and secondary windows; reset-after seconds
- `additional_rate_limits`, a map keyed by model name (bounded by models on the plan)
- credits balance / has_credits / unlimited

Data-quality metrics, so the pipeline reports its own trustworthiness:
- `critical_path.coverage` = `complete` vs `missing_harness_boundary` (4.6% of responses)
- `baseline_reset` count - cold-start deltas are upper bounds, not measurements, and dashboards
  wanting accuracy must be able to exclude them

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Cumulative temporality; restart produces a clean counter reset rather than a spike or a gap.
- [ ] Attributes come from the attribute-contract package only.
- [ ] Rate-limit gauges are per-account; a test asserts they are never aggregated across accounts.
- [ ] Prewarm and compaction excluded from user-turn counts, asserted by test.
- [ ] Instrument names checked against current OTel gen_ai semantic conventions.

body:
## Why

Loki's `max_line_size` defaults to **256KB** and the validation error is `line_too_long`. Unless the
tenant sets `max_line_size_truncate: true`, the line is **discarded entirely** - verified against
current Loki docs (`operations/request-validation-rate-limits.md`).

That is worse than it sounds. `response.instructions` reaches 67KB and tool outputs are the single
largest content source in the capture. A turn record that bundles metadata and content into one JSON
line does not lose the oversized part - it loses the **whole record**, so the token counts, the model
attribution and the latency go with the stdout that overflowed it.

Separately, `per_stream_rate_limit` defaults to 3MB/s per stream with a 15MB burst. Every turn
sharing one label set means one stream, so a burst of large tool outputs can be rejected wholesale.

The decision on content is unchanged and settled: **everything ships**. This issue is only about not
losing it silently.

## Scope

- Content emitted on its own lines, structurally separate from the turn metadata record, so an
  oversized body costs that body and nothing else.
- A configured per-line byte budget below `max_line_size`, applied to each emitted line. Truncation
  is explicit: an unambiguous marker plus the untruncated length, which `ToolOutput.Chars` and
  `Truncated` already model at the reducer level.
- Loki 4xx responses parsed and counted **by reason** (`line_too_long`, `rate_limited`,
  `out_of_order`, `stream_limit`), exposed as a metric. A swallowed 4xx is how "we have been dropping
  5% of lines for a month" happens.
- Stream count kept low by construction - this is the same constraint driving the label decision in
  the attribute-contract issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No emitted line exceeds the configured budget; test feeds the corpus and asserts the maximum.
- [ ] A turn whose tool output overflows still emits its metadata record intact - the test asserts
      the metadata survives, which is the whole point.
- [ ] Truncation is marked and the original length preserved.
- [ ] Rejections counted by reason and surfaced as a metric, with a test against a stub returning
      each 4xx shape.
- [ ] Measured peak line size and stream count recorded on this issue.

Part of #5.
title: Never silently lose a Loki line to max_line_size or a rate limit

body:
## Why

Phase P3 of #1. The archive is the only place the full conversation exists; everything else in the
stack has metadata only.

## Scope

Batched push to `https://logs-prod-035.grafana.net/loki/api/v1/push` (user `<LOKI_TENANT_ID>`, `glc_` token),
direct, no Alloy hop.

**Record types**, each its own line so one oversized body cannot destroy the rest (see the line-size
issue):
- turn metadata (the `Turn` struct minus content arrays)
- prompts (user / developer / assistant, deduplicated as already implemented)
- assistant messages
- tool calls and tool outputs
- agent messages (author -> recipient; 191 distinct pairs observed)
- transport events (close codes, frame errors)
- error events
- distinct instruction bodies, emitted once against the LRU

**Labels and structured metadata** come from the attribute-contract issue, not from this one.

Timestamps must be the record's own, not ingest time - the reducer already carries `FirstTS`,
`LastTS`, `ServerCreatedAt`, `ServerCompletedAt` and the client's `TurnStart`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Batched push with retry and backoff; a permanent 4xx is counted and dropped, not retried
      forever.
- [ ] Push failure does not advance the checkpoint.
- [ ] Timestamps are source timestamps, monotonic within a stream.
- [ ] Content dedup verified end to end: replaying the corpus emits each distinct instruction body
      once and each prompt once, as `TestReducer_InputContentIsDeduplicated` already asserts at the
      reducer level.
- [ ] Emitted volume measured against the 13-hour projection (~54MB/day) and recorded on this issue.

body:
## Why

Everything built so far is libraries and analysis tools. There is no service: no binary that runs
continuously, no configuration, no shutdown path. P3/P4 have nowhere to plug in until this exists.

## Scope

- `cmd/codexlb2otel` - long-running process wiring `internal/tail` to the sinks.
- Config file with `${ENV}` and `file:` secret references, following `genai-otel-bridge`'s existing
  scheme rather than inventing a second one. Secrets never inline, never logged.
- Config covers: archive directory, checkpoint path, poll interval, chunk size, `DeleteAfter`
  (reclaim; defaults to zero = never delete, and stays opt-in because it removes the only copy of
  the raw capture), sink endpoints and credentials, batch sizes and flush intervals.
- Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM, stop polling, flush in-flight batches, persist the checkpoint, exit.
  A checkpoint written before a failed flush would silently lose turns.
- Structured logging via `log/slog`, level configurable.
- Health/readiness endpoint on loopback.
- Config validation at startup that fails loudly rather than starting half-wired.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Binary starts from a config file, tails a directory, and exits cleanly on SIGTERM.
- [ ] Secrets resolve from `${ENV}` and `file:` refs; a test asserts a secret value never appears in
      log output or in the health endpoint.
- [ ] Shutdown flushes before persisting the checkpoint, and a test proves a failed flush does not
      advance it (the existing `TestWatcher_FailedEmitDoesNotAdvanceCheckpoint` invariant, at the
      service level).
- [ ] Invalid config fails at startup with a message naming the field.

Blocks #1 P3 and P4.

body:
## Why

`internal/turn.Turn` carries ~90 fields. P3 (Loki), P4 (OTLP metrics) and P7 (traces) each need to
decide independently which of those become metric attributes, which become Loki labels, which become
structured metadata, and which become span attributes. If they decide separately they will disagree,
and a metric label chosen wrongly is a cardinality incident rather than a cosmetic problem.

This is the shared seam. It must be frozen before the emit phases fan out.

## Ground truth already established (do not re-derive)

Verified across 1.32M records / 6,936 turns, and re-confirmed on the 2026-08-07 corpus:

**Safe as metric attributes** - bounded, measured:

| attribute | observed values |
|---|---|
| `model` | 6 (`gpt-5.6-terra`, `gpt-5.6-sol`, `gpt-5.3-codex-spark`, `gpt-5.6-sol-wm`, `gpt-5.4-mini`, `gpt-5.6-luna`) |
| `reasoning_effort` | 4 (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`) |
| `status` | 4 (`completed`, `incomplete`, `transport`, `error`) |
| `request_kind` | 3 (`turn`, `prewarm`, `compaction`) |
| `family` | 3 (`websocket`, `http`, `probe`) |
| `thread_source` | 2 (`user`, `subagent`) |
| `service_tier` | 2 (`default`, `auto`) |
| `plan_type` | 2 (`pro`, `business`) |
| `account_id` | 3 |
| `tool_name` | 9 + a `collaboration` namespace of 6 |
| `error_type` / `error_code` | 2 / 3 |
| `critical_path.coverage` | 2 (`complete`, `missing_harness_boundary`) |

**Never a metric attribute** - unbounded or rotating:
`thread_id`, `response_id`, `request_id`, `session_id`, `turn_id`, `logical_turn_id`, `trace_id`,
`span_id`, `window_id`, `installation_id`, `prompt_cache_key`, `engine_ids` (rotates, and can be a
comma-joined list), `error_message` (embeds ids), `safety_identifier`.

**Decisions to make in this issue**
- `account_id` as a metric attribute: yes. codex-lb load-balances across 3 accounts and per-account
  rate-limit headroom is arguably the headline metric; averaging across accounts hides the exhaustion
  it exists to show.
- `safety_identifier` maps 1:1 to a human. Log/structured-metadata only, never a metric attribute,
  never a Loki label.
- Loki labels stay minimal (`service_name`, `family`, `record_type`). Everything else is structured
  metadata - Loki labels are a stream cardinality multiplier, and `per_stream_rate_limit` is 3MB/s.
- Whether `model` belongs in Loki labels at all, given it multiplies streams by 6.

## Scope

- A single package (`internal/attr` or similar) owning the mapping, imported by every emitter, so
  there is exactly one definition.
- OTel semantic-convention alignment where one exists: prefer `gen_ai.*` (`gen_ai.request.model`,
  `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, ...) over invented names. Check the current spec rather than assuming;
  `genai-otel-bridge` is the in-house reference for what was chosen there.
- A runtime guard: attributes are emitted from an allowlist, and anything outside it is counted and
  dropped rather than passed through. A new model appearing must not be able to become an unbounded
  label if the value ever turns into something id-shaped.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One package defines the Turn -> {metric attribute, Loki label, structured metadata, span
      attribute} mapping; no emitter constructs attribute sets of its own.
- [ ] Every metric attribute is on the measured-bounded list above, with its observed cardinality
      recorded in a comment.
- [ ] Runtime allowlist enforced at emit, with a counter for rejected attributes.
- [ ] Test asserts the allowlist matches the corpus: reduce the corpus, assert every emitted
      attribute value set is within its documented bound.
- [ ] `safety_identifier` provably cannot reach a metric attribute or a Loki label.
- [ ] Naming checked against current OTel gen_ai semantic conventions, with deviations justified.

Blocks #1 P3, P4 and the traces phase.

**Four distinct ids, one confusing label.** codex-lb's UI calls `resp_*` the "Request ID". The
archive's `request_id` is a different value. Whatever the contract names these, it must not
perpetuate the collision - see #15.

codexlb.request_kind              4/8  [compaction memory prewarm turn]
codexlb.family                    3/8  [http unknown websocket]
gen_ai.request.reasoning.level    4/8  [high low medium xhigh]
codexlb.account_id               2/16  [bd537096-… c423f6b9-…]
codexlb.plan_type                 2/8  [business pro]
codexlb.service_tier              2/8  [auto default]
codexlb.thread_source             3/8  [memory_consolidation subagent user]
codexlb.subagent_kind             2/8  [memory_consolidation thread_spawn]
codexlb.originator               2/16  [codex-tui codex_exec]
error.type                       1/32  [invalid_request_error]
codexlb.error_code               2/64  [previous_response_not_found websocket_connection_limit_reached]
codexlb.critical_path.coverage    2/8  [complete missing_harness_boundary]

body:
Build a long-running Go service that tails codex-lb's conversation-archive gzip files, derives model/agent telemetry, and emits OTLP metrics and Loki logs directly to Grafana Cloud.

## Why a new repo

`genai-otel-bridge` is the nearest sibling but is **content-free by design** — it never requests prompt/response bodies and enforces that as a release gate. Shipping full conversation history would violate its core invariant. It stays the architectural reference (OTLP emit, `${ENV}`/`file:` secret refs, self-observing), not the home.

## Ground truth (verified 2026-08-06, do not re-derive)

Established against three live archive hours: 275MB gz, 1,245 responses, 87 logical turns, 25 threads.

### Archive format
- `<dir>/<YYYY-MM-DD>T<HH>.jsonl.gz`, rotated hourly by UTC hour.
- **Multi-member gzip via `O_APPEND`** — `_write_gzip_jsonl_records` closes a complete gzip member per batch. Verified 15,106 self-contained members in one 16MB file, ~1.1 records each. This is what makes safe tailing possible.
- Records: `{account_id, direction, extra, headers, kind, method, payload:{text}, request_id, status_code, timestamp, transport, url}`. `payload.text` is a JSON string needing separate parsing.
- **The writer silently drops records under disk pressure** (`_archive_disk_pressure_active()`). Gaps are expected; never treat as corruption.
- `conversation_archive_enabled` defaults to `False` — opt-in per deployment.
- Headers are pre-redacted (`Authorization: [redacted]`).

### Two traps
1. **`responsesapi.websocket_timing` is CUMULATIVE per logical turn** (`timing_scope: "logical_turn"`). `num_engine_calls`, `total_turn_time_s`, `engine_*_tokens_total`, `num_sampled_tokens_total`, `client_tool_pause_total_ms` accumulate and reset at the next turn. Naive summing overcounts ~5.7x. Must diff within a thread; boundary = when `num_engine_calls` fails to advance. Validated across 87 turns: zero negative deltas, delta-engine-prompt / usage-input = **0.9996**. `usage.*` from `response.completed` is per-response and safe to use directly.
2. **`x-codex-turn-metadata` is stale** — reports `request_kind: "prewarm"` on every frame, stamped at connect time, never updated. Never filter on it. (Distinct from the Postgres `request_kind`, which is client-set but genuine per-request.)

### Not recoverable
`reasoning.encrypted_content` and inter-agent `message` payloads are Fernet encrypted **by OpenAI with OpenAI's key** — codex-lb's own `encryption.key` returns `InvalidToken`. Only token counts and author/recipient routing survive. Do not attempt decryption.

### Cardinality
- `engine_ids` can be a **comma-joined list** and rotates (6 values in 3h). Never a metric label — log field only.
- `thread_id` / `response_id` / `request_id` / `session_id` / `trace_id` / `logical_turn_id` are unbounded: Loki structured metadata only.
- Safe metric attributes: `model`, `role` (main|subagent), `reasoning_effort`, `status`, `plan`, `verbosity`, `service_tier`, `tool_name`.

### Division of labour — what NOT to build
- codex-lb already exposes **60 Prometheus metric families** on loopback `:19090`, all proxy-internals. Do not duplicate.
- Postgres `request_logs` already has cost_usd, latency, tokens, service tier, error codes, and drives the `codex-lb-overview` dashboard. Do not re-derive.
- Postgres is an **enrichment** source only: attach `cost_usd` / `account_id` / `api_key_id` to archive turns, which the wire data cannot know.

## Decisions made
- Private repo.
- **Direct push for both metrics and logs** — no Alloy hop. OTLP to `https://otlp-gateway-prod-gb-south-1.grafana.net/otlp` (instance `<GRAFANA_STACK_ID>`); Loki to `https://logs-prod-035.grafana.net/loki/api/v1/push` (user `<LOKI_TENANT_ID>`). Both use the `glc_` token.
- **No backfill** — tail from current files forward.
- Full conversation content IS shipped (deliberate; anything the agent printed lands in Loki).

## Phases

This issue is the tracker. Each phase now has its own issue; progress and decisions live there.

- [x] **P1 - reader.** Multi-member gzip tailer with byte-offset resume. `833948d`
- [x] **P1b - watcher + checkpoint store.** `a4ee197`
- [x] **P2 - reducer.** Frame typing, logical-turn state machine, cumulative->delta. `aa9b8b5`, `6719bb3`
- [x] **Format-drift detection.** `clbprobe` + committed content-free baseline. `e3cb67d`
- [x] #3 - **freeze the Turn -> telemetry attribute contract**. `internal/attr`, validated over the whole corpus `7f57ff8`
- [x] #4 - **service skeleton**: `cmd/codexlb2otel`, config, lifecycle. `78ab065`
- [x] #5 - **P3 Loki emit**. `c035046`
- [x] #6 - never silently lose a Loki line to `max_line_size` or a rate limit. `c035046`
- [x] #7 - **P4 OTLP metrics**. `eb0b7b0`
- [ ] #8 - self-observability, ingest lag above all
- [ ] #9 - **P5 Postgres enrichment**
- [ ] #10 - **P6 packaging and release**
- [x] #11 - **P7 traces to Tempo** (promoted from out-of-scope, see below). `1479195`, semconv `954bd03`
- [ ] #12 - adopt the `timing_metrics` domains still being dropped
- [ ] #13 - run the drift probe on a schedule and alert on it
- [ ] #14 - dashboards and alerts as code
- [x] #16 - reduce frames to per-response turns with cumulative-metric deltas. `a7464ee`
- [x] #17 - surface websocket connection health. `7f57ff8`
- [x] #18 - GenAI semantic-convention compliance. `954bd03`
- [x] #19 - emit Generations to Grafana sigil / agento11y. `d4cfe31`
- [x] #20 - corpus drift: the concurrent-series token over-count. `a052040`
- [ ] #21 - `clbprobe` is blind to embedded JSON documents
- [ ] #22 - sigil/semconv follow-ups (items 3 and 5 done, `a13a574`)

## Out of scope
Re-deriving `request_logs` or codex-lb's own metrics; decrypting reasoning; replacing
`codex-lb-overview`.

**Backfill/replay remains out of scope** - reaffirmed 2026-08-07. The corpus is a test and analysis
fixture, never an ingest source; the service tails forward only.

**Traces are NO LONGER out of scope.** They were parked here on the grounds that the evidence was
only `traceparent` and a trace-shaped agent tree. Full-corpus profiling since has turned up the
server `turn_id`, `previous_response_id` chaining responses into a DAG, `parent_thread_id` /
`forked_from_thread_id`, `turn_started_at_unix_ms`, a per-response `critical_path` breakdown and a
per-tool-call duration array - a complete trace model. Promoted to #11, sequenced after #5 and #7.

comments.body:
## P1 + P2 landed

`internal/archive` (multi-member gzip tailer) and `internal/turn` (reducer) are in. All 10 tests pass against the three captured hours.

**P1 — reader.** `DecodeMembers` decodes only complete gzip members and reports the input bytes they covered, so a checkpoint offset never lands mid-member. A truncated trailing member returns cleanly (that is the normal steady state while codex-lb is mid-append); genuine corruption errors but preserves the good prefix so a caller can still make progress.

Implementation note worth keeping: it decodes over a `bytes.Reader` deliberately, because that implements `io.ByteReader` so `compress/gzip` will not wrap it in a `bufio` and cannot read ahead past a member trailer. That is what makes the offset arithmetic exact.

Verified against a real hour: 15,106 members / 16,552 lines pinned, and a two-pass decode from a mid-member cut is byte-identical to a single pass.

**P2 — reducer.** Cumulative→delta conversion validated: **zero negative deltas** across 1,245 responses / 87 logical turns / 25 threads, and summed engine-prompt deltas track per-response usage at **0.9996**. `TestReducer_StateSurvivesRestart` confirms 1,079 turns come out identical across a snapshot/restore cycle.

### Two deliberate divergences from the Python reference
- **Model attribution.** The reference read the model only from `response.completed`, leaving the 9 responses that never completed as `None`. This reducer also reads `response.create`/`created`, so all 1,245 are attributed (643 sol / 602 terra) and none is blank. Test pins the *higher* numbers on purpose.
- **Logical-turn ids for timing-less responses.** Prewarm responses do no engine work and carry no cumulative series, so each becomes its own logical turn rather than being left unassigned.

### Findings added since the issue was written
- `engine_ids` observed **6 distinct values across 3 hours** and can be a comma-joined list — confirms it must stay a log field, never a metric attribute. Asserted in `TestReducer_CardinalityAssumptions`.
- Responses can end without `response.completed` (9 in the sample). `Flush`/`Evict` handle them; without eviction the open-response map would leak.

- [x] P1 — reader
- [ ] P1b — watcher + checkpoint store
- [x] P2 — reducer

Next: P1b (directory watcher + persisted checkpoint), then P3 (Loki emit).

## Storage decision: Loki + OTLP to Grafana Cloud. No ClickHouse.

Measured against 13 hours of live archive rather than the earlier 3-hour sample.

| | |
|---|---|
| Input | 1,162.8 MB compressed / 13 h (~2.1 GB/day) |
| Frames | 1,277,434 lines in 1,039,669 gzip members |
| Responses | 6,618 across 419 logical turns, 93 threads |
| **Reduced output** | **29.4 MB JSON, 6.1 MB gzipped / 13 h** |
| Projected | ~54 MB/day, ~1.6 GB/month |

**Verdict: ClickHouse is not justified.** The reduction is 2.53% of input, so ~1.6 GB/month reaches the sinks — Loki absorbs that without noticing. ClickHouse would add a stateful service needing backups (a Backrest plan), upgrades, monitoring and a datasource, to store data that fits in the existing paid platform a hundred times over. Grafana Cloud is already provisioned, already has the `codex-lb-overview` dashboard, and `gcx` is already wired.

## Temporality: cumulative, confirmed

Mimir 3.0 does have **native delta OTLP ingestion**, but its own docs mark it experimental — "early stage of development, ingestion and querying subject to change", "use with caution in production" — and it is not enableable on managed Grafana Cloud. The supported path is cumulative; `deltatocumulative` is the conversion hop for delta-only sources.

This simplifies us. The reducer already emits per-response **deltas**, which are the natural argument to an OTel `Counter.Add()`. The SDK aggregates to cumulative for export, and a restart resets the counter with a fresh start time — correct counter-reset semantics. **Metrics therefore need no checkpoint.** The checkpoint exists only for within-turn delta correctness and for not re-shipping logs.

## What the wider corpus exposed

**A decoding bug that was silently discarding data.** `inputItem.Output` was typed `string`, but the protocol sends a list of parts 346 times against 95 as a string. Go's json decoder aborts the **whole event** on one mismatched field, so a single unexpected shape discarded every prompt, the model, the effort and the input count for that entire turn — and the `response.created` fallback refilled the model, masking it. Recovered input items went 148 → 1,650 across the fixtures. Both polymorphic fields are now held raw and flattened leniently.

**`error` events, 100% unhandled.** They carry `server_is_overloaded`, `websocket_connection_limit_reached` (the 60-minute connection cap), `previous_response_not_found` and tool-call desync. Critically **no `response.completed` follows one**, so these turns previously sat open until evicted and were reported as merely incomplete, losing the reason. Two of the six also arrived with **no `request_id` at all**; those are now handled standalone instead of merging under a `""` key into one ever-growing turn.

**Wall-clock eviction would have misfired on every restart.** Evicting in-flight responses against `time.Now()` means catching up on a backlog evicts everything on the first pass purely because the archive is hours old — while the completions sit in the next chunk. Now measured against the newest record *seen*. Found by the incremental-append test, not by inspection.

**Cold-start deltas are upper bounds, not measurements.** A response whose turn began before we started watching absorbs all the unobserved work. Previously indistinguishable from a real delta; now flagged `baseline_reset` so dashboards can exclude it. `MaxThreadGap` (30 min) additionally resets a stale baseline rather than diffing across a gap where counters advanced unseen.

**Two `request_id` namespaces** coexist — `ws_<hex32>` (4,558/h) and bare UUID (12,210/h) — on the same transport carrying the same event types. Not a bug; both are valid keys, do not "fix" this.

## Content capture

`response.create` re-sends the entire thread every turn (arrays up to 886 items; 371 MB of the 1.16 GB, the largest single event type) and is the **only** place user prompts and tool results appear. Emitted on first sighting only, against a bounded LRU. Developer/`instructions` prompts dedupe globally (identical boilerplate; one 66 KB preamble stored once, not once per thread); user/assistant dedupe per thread so each thread still reconstructs in full. **The entire input side of 371 MB costs 8.6 MB.**

## Cardinality (guarded by test)

Safe as metric attributes: model (5), reasoning effort, status (3), tool name (9), error type/code. Log fields only: every id, `engine_ids` (rotates, can be a joined list), `error_message` (embeds ids).

Measured by pushing one line per age and **querying each back** — not by reading the status code:

2. **That 400 was swallowed.** The "permanent 4xx is counted and dropped" rule is correct for a verdict on the *data* (`line_too_long`, `out_of_order`) and wrong for a verdict on the *service* (malformed request, auth) — the latter rejects every future push identically, so dropping means running forever delivering nothing. Those now return an error and hold the checkpoint.

The reason all of this stayed hidden: rejection counts lived inside the sink struct and nothing printed them. `reportRejections` now logs every non-zero reason at WARN on shutdown.

### Contract gaps the lanes found, all closed in 14391e7

- `attr.With` was a bare function and therefore the one path around the cardinality guard — two of three sinks took it, for exactly the attributes that cannot be derived from a Turn (`tool_name`, `token_type`). Now a `Guard` method; off-contract keys are dropped and counted.
- `attr.FrameType` had no field and no source. Now derived from `FrameErrors`/`CloseCode`; `TransportEvent` joins as identity-class so the reason prose reaches Loki.
- One shared `attr.Guard` across all sinks — three would each admit 32 models and triple the real ceiling.

### Deviations worth knowing

- **Traces do not use the captured traceparent as the trace id.** It is connection-scoped: 8 of 21 threads in one archive hour carried two distinct captured ids because the websocket reconnected. Rooting on it splits one conversation into two traces. Trace id is `hash(ThreadID)`; the captured traceparent becomes a span Link.
- **Token `total` is not emitted.** `reasoning` and `cached` are nested breakdowns of `output`/`input`, so summing across `gen_ai.token.type` would double-count.
- **`gen_ai.client.token.usage` is specified as a histogram; token totals here are counters** under `codexlb.*` names. The convention's name is not reused for a differently-typed instrument.

### Not done, and stated rather than skipped

- Streaming-shape instruments (text-delta count, time-between-tokens, pause count) — `Turn` carries the fields, `names.go` defines no instrument. Follow-up.
- Credits gauges are implemented but **unverified against real data**: zero `credits` blocks exist anywhere in the corpus.
- The service is not yet installed as a unit on camden; it has only been run in the foreground.

Filed #18 (GenAI semconv compliance - several `codexlb.*` names have standard equivalents) and #19 (Grafana sigil/agento11y support). Fixed en route in 228c717: no span carried `gen_ai.operation.name` or `gen_ai.provider.name`, so every span was invisible to any convention-aware consumer while the exporter reported success.

## Phase update — 2026-08-07

Every emit phase is now closed. The service reduces archives into turns and ships to four destinations: Loki (native, never OTLP logs), OTLP metrics, OTLP traces, and Grafana sigil Generations.

**Closed since the last update:** #16 `a7464ee`, #20 `a052040`, #18 `954bd03`, #19 `d4cfe31`, #3 + #17 `7f57ff8`. Plus #22 items 3 and 5 in `a13a574` (that issue stays open for items 1, 2 and 4).

### The correction that matters most

**#20 was a silent 4.3× engine-token over-count, and it passed the existing guard test.** A thread does not run one cumulative counter series — `request_kind` values `turn`, `prewarm`, `compaction` and `memory` run *concurrently* on the same `thread_id`, each with its own counters starting from `num_engine_calls=1`. Diffing them against one shared baseline attributed a whole series to a single response of another. The only visible symptom was a negative *sampled*-token delta on twelve turns, and only because sampled tokens happen to be the one counter where the memory series runs ahead. The token over-count itself was silent. Fixed by `turn.seriesKey = thread_id + request_kind`; state version 1→2 (v1 keys cannot be migrated, so a v1 snapshot is discarded).

**The second-order lesson, now applied in three places:** a passing guard test and a covered case are different things. `TestReducer_NoNegativeDeltas` read the three cheapest archives and none of the twelve affected turns was in them. `internal/attr`'s cap test read two of fourteen. Both now read the whole corpus, and #21 exists because the drift probe had the same blind spot from a different direction.

### Other corrections worth not re-deriving

- **Three of #18's five proposed OTel renames did not exist.** Real names: `gen_ai.request.reasoning.level` (not `thinking.level`), `gen_ai.server.time_to_first_token` (not `gen_ai.client.*`), and there is no `server_tool_use` / web-search concept at all, so `codexlb.web_search_requests` keeps its name. The conventions live in `open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai`; the copies in `open-telemetry/semantic-conventions` are deprecated. Check the spec, never recall it — the tables in these issues have now been wrong three times.
- **An empty `request_id` is not the HTTP family.** It was being classified as HTTP because it was "not prefixed `ws_`", so connection-level close and error frames — websockets dying — were booked as HTTP-family errors. Now `FamilyUnknown`.
- **`x-request-id` is not the record's `request_id`.** They agree on 5,685 of 22,837; the header is connection-scoped and goes stale exactly like `x-codex-turn-metadata`.
- **`temperature` and `top_p` are on the wire and do vary.** #18 recorded them as absent, which was wrong; only `max_output_tokens` is genuinely null. Deferred to #22 item 2 because `Turn` has no field for either — a scope boundary, not a data judgment.
- **A 2xx is not delivery, in all three protocols now.** Loki returns 204 for a line it discarded; sigil's OTLP path reports `partial_success`; agento11y returns per-item `accepted` verdicts. Every sink parses the body.
- **Not every permanent 4xx should hold the checkpoint.** A 413 is permanent like a 401 but caused by the *data*, so treating it as a config fault wedges the pipeline forever on a batch that can never drain. It is a data fault — and since `a13a574` it is halved and retried before anything is counted.

1. **#21** — the probe is blind to embedded JSON documents (in progress)
2. **#12** + **#22 items 1–2** — timing domains, tool catalogue, request params. All three edit `internal/turn`, so they go to one owner, not in parallel.
3. **#8** self-observability, then **#13** scheduled probe, **#14** dashboards and alerts (now also carrying #17's connection-limit alert), **#15** lookup UX
4. **#9** Postgres enrichment
5. **#10** packaging — last, and gated. Docker + compose into codex-lb's services, not systemd. Nothing is deployed yet, by instruction.

## Phase update — parallel wave

Six issues closed since the last update, run as concurrent lanes with disjoint file ownership.

**Closed:** #23 + #15 `4ac0e92`, #21 `4d94522`, #12 `4968921`, #22 `a13a574` + `4968921`, #13 `69f4fb3`, #3 + #17 `7f57ff8`. Plus `198d9d0` (Loki budget measured over the whole corpus) and `d9992b5` (a CI-only test bug).

**This repo now has CI for the first time**, and it is green.

### Corrections worth not re-deriving

- **`go run` collapses every non-zero exit code to 1.** It does not propagate. The drift probe's four documented exit codes are load-bearing in CI, and running it through `go run` made the no-corpus case look like breaking drift on every run. Build the binary.
- **A `sync.Once` around a corpus reduction breaks the no-corpus skip.** `fixture.All` skips when no corpus is present, a skip is a `runtime.Goexit`, and inside a `Once` that marks it done with an empty cache — so the first test skipped correctly and every later one asserted against zero turns. This is how the first CI run failed. The error path inside the same helper had already been guarded against exactly this; the skip path had not, because it had not been thought about.
- **`clbprobe` has no `-full` flag.** A full scan is the default when `-sampled` is omitted. The issues said otherwise.
- **The archive's `workspaces` block is keyed by absolute filesystem path.** Descending into embedded JSON for #21 put a home-directory layout, private repository names and a personal forge hostname into a generated `corpus.sig.json`. No existing guard could catch it — `contentSafe` screens values by the name of the segment above them, and there the user's data *is* the segment name. Found by auditing the generated file, not by a test.
- **`temperature` and `top_p` do not vary** (26,691 occurrences, one value each), and **the tool catalogue is not on `response.create`** — it is nested in an `additional_tools` input item on 5.2% of creates, and `output_schema` does not exist. Both were asserted otherwise by #22.
- **Every `taas_*` field is absent or null**, so #12's headline "separate provider wait from generation time" is not achievable from this capture.
- **`request_logs.archive_request_id` joins at 100%** across all 8,931 turns, both id namespaces — but **it has no index**, so the natural join key would full-table-scan 53,454 rows per cache miss against production. See #9.
